passages.title: The Criterion sent down by the true King
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the opening declaration of Sūrah al-Furqān: Allah praises Himself for the Book He has sent down, names Himself as the sole King of everything that exists, and then exposes the foolishness of worshipping anything beside Him. What holds them together is a single argument — the One who sent this Book is the One who owns and made and measured all things, so nothing that is itself made can ever deserve your worship.

## The setting of the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a consensus among the commentators that this sūrah was revealed in Makkah. Where they differ is over a few of its verses: Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah held that three verses are Madanī and the rest Makkan, while Qurṭubī and a few others held the reverse — that the sūrah is Madanī with only a few verses Makkan.

That matters for how you read the opening. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises the sūrah's subject as describing and defining the greatness of the Holy Qurʼān and the truth of the Prophet's ﷺ prophethood — the two things the disbelievers had expressed doubts about — and says the sūrah contains answers to their objections. So notice what ayah 1 does *not* do. It does not begin by arguing. It begins by blessing the One who sent the Book down.

## "Tabāraka" — a blessedness that never runs out

The sūrah opens with **تَبَارَكَ**, *tabāraka*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces it to *baraka*, meaning abundance of a good thing, and reports Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation of this first verse: **all blessings are from Allah alone**. Ibn Kathīr adds a point about the shape of the word itself — this verbal form implies a blessing that is ongoing, permanent, eternal. Not a burst of good that came and went, but goodness that keeps welling up because it belongs to the One who is its source.

Ibn Kathīr reads the whole opening as Allah praising Himself for the Noble Qurʼān He has revealed to His noble Messenger ﷺ, and points to a parallel opening: *"All the praises and thanks be to Allah, Who has sent down to His servant the Book, and has not placed therein any crookedness. (He has made it) straight to give warning of a severe punishment from Him, and to give glad tidings to the believers, who do righteous deeds…"* (18:1–2). The same elements sit in both places: Allah praised, the Book sent down, "His servant," and a warning.

## "Nazzala" — why the Qurʼān came down in pieces

The verse does not say *anzala* (sent down) but **نَزَّلَ**, *nazzala*. Ibn Kathīr explains that this form implies something done a great deal and often — repeatedly, in instalments. He points to 4:136, where both verbs appear side by side in a single ayah: *"And the Book which He (nazzala) sent down to His Messenger, and the Scripture which He (anzala) sent down to those before (him)."* The switch is deliberate. Each of the earlier Books was sent down at one time; the Qurʼān was revealed gradually, in stages — ayat after ayat, rulings after rulings, sūrahs after sūrahs.

And Ibn Kathīr says this staged descent is not a lesser way of revealing but a greater one: it is more eloquent, and indicative of greater care for the one to whom it is revealed. Allah Himself makes that point later in this same sūrah, answering the objection head-on:

> *"And those who disbelieve say: 'Why is not the Qurʼān revealed to him all at once?' Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby. And We have revealed it to you gradually, in stages. And no example or similitude do they bring, but We reveal to you the truth, and the better explanation thereof."* (25:32–33)

So the very feature the disbelievers objected to — that revelation kept arriving in pieces rather than landing as one finished scroll — is the feature the Qurʼān names as care. Two words are worth holding onto here, and both come from the sources rather than from us: Ibn Kathīr's phrase for staged revelation is *greater care*, and the ayah's own phrase is *that We may strengthen your heart thereby*. If guidance has reached you slowly, over years rather than all at once, those are the two words the Qurʼān itself puts on that experience.

## "Al-Furqān" — the Book that separates

Ibn Kathīr says the sūrah was named al-Furqān because the Qurʼān is the criterion that decides between truth and falsehood, guidance and misguidance, right and wrong, lawful and unlawful. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word from its root sense of *distinguishing*: the Qurʼān by its very nature distinguishes between right and wrong, and differentiates, through miracles, between the right people and the wrong ones — which is why it is called Furqān. A criterion does not merely inform you; it sorts. Held up against it, positions divide and so do people.

Ibn Kathīr describes the Book being praised here as *"this great, detailed, clear Book"* about which Allah says: *"Falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it, (it is) sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise"* (41:42). That is why it can function as a criterion at all: a standard that could itself be corrupted would be no standard.

## "ʿAbdihi" — the title of highest honour

Allah does not say "to His Prophet" or "to Muḥammad" but **عَلَىٰ عَبْدِهِ**, *to His servant*. Ibn Kathīr calls this a description of praise and commendation, because Allah is here connecting him to Himself, describing him as His servant. And he shows that Allah describes him this way precisely at the highest moments:

- At the Night of the Isrāʼ, which Ibn Kathīr calls the noblest of events: *"Glorified be He Who took His servant for a journey by night"* (17:1).
- When describing how he stood and called upon his Lord: *"And when the servant of Allah stood up invoking Him, they (the jinn) just made round him a dense crowd"* (72:19).
- And here, where Allah describes how the Book is revealed to him and how the angel comes down to him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the same point: by addressing the one on whom the Book was revealed as *ʿabdahu*, His slave, at the very beginning of the sūrah, his honoured position is highlighted — and there cannot be a greater honour for anyone than to be called by Allah "His own."

This is worth sitting with. In a passage whose whole purpose is to answer people who had cast doubt on his prophethood, the title Allah selects for him is *His servant* — and the two commentators read that title the same way: as praise, and as an honour beyond which there is nothing greater. That is where the honour is located. Not somewhere past servanthood, but inside it.

## "A warner to all the worlds"

The purpose clause in ayah 1 is **لِيَكُونَ لِلْعَالَمِينَ نَذِيرًا** — that he may be a warner to all nations. Ibn Kathīr's reading is that he alone has been blessed with this great, detailed, clear Book, and that the One who made it the mighty criterion singled him out to convey it to those who seek the shade of trees and to those who live on the land — that is, to all of mankind, nomad and settled alike.

He cites the Prophet's ﷺ own words on this: *"I have been sent to the red and the black."* And: *"I have been given five things which no Prophet before me was given"* — among which he mentioned, *"[Before me] a Prophet was sent only to his own people, but I have been sent to all of mankind."* (Ibn Kathīr does not name a collection for either report in this material, so they are passed on here exactly as he gives them, without attribution to a named book.) Maʿārif ul Qurʼān separately notes a ḥadīth recorded in **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim** in which the Prophet ﷺ pointed out six special features of his prophethood, one of them being its universality — that it is for all ages and all people.

The Qurʼān itself states it plainly: *"Say: 'O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah…'"* (7:158). And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes *lil-ʿālamīn* here as proof that his prophethood was for the entire universe, and not just for a certain community or time, as was the case with other prophets.

Notice too the word chosen: *nadhīr*, a **warner**. That is the note struck first. A criterion that separates truth from falsehood is good news only if you are on the right side of the line; the first duty of the one carrying it is to tell people that the line is real.

## Ayah 2: whose Book this is

Ibn Kathīr links ayah 2 straight back to the messengership of ayah 1: the meaning of "I am sent to you all" is that *the One who has sent me is the Sovereign of the heaven and the earth, who merely says to a thing "Be!" and it is; He is the One who gives life and causes death.* A universal message needs a universal Sender. If the Lord of everything speaks, His speech is addressed to everything He owns.

So ayah 2 names Him: **الَّذِي لَهُ مُلْكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ** — *He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth* — **وَلَمْ يَتَّخِذْ وَلَدًا وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُ شَرِيكٌ فِي الْمُلْكِ** — *and who has begotten no son and for whom there is no partner in the dominion.* Ibn Kathīr's comment is brief and decisive: Allah states that He is above having any offspring or partner. The two denials answer the two ways people have always tried to soften Allah's exclusivity — by giving Him a family, or by giving Him colleagues.

## "He created everything and measured it exactly"

**خَلَقَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ فَقَدَّرَهُ تَقْدِيرًا.** Ibn Kathīr: everything apart from Him is created and subject to Him; He is the Creator, Lord, Master and Deity of all things, and everything is subject to His dominion, control and power.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up why *taqdīr* (designing in a perfect measure) is mentioned **after** *khalq* (creation), since they are two distinct acts:

- **Khalq** is to create something from nothing — to bring something into being without any pre-existing substance whatsoever.
- **Taqdīr** is that whatever has been created, its components, appearance, properties and signs are made to suit the purpose of its creation.

Then it gives the examples, which are worth reading slowly because they turn an abstract attribute into something you can touch:

- The **sky** — its form, its constituents and its shape — conforms to the purpose for which Allah created it; the stars and planets likewise possess those qualities for which they were created.
- The **earth** is not made in such a liquid form that anything put on it is drowned, nor made too hard, like steel or concrete, to be dug. It is made in solid form and given a hardness such that it can be dug — to take out underground water, or to lay foundations for buildings.
- **Water** is given the liquid form, itself full of divine wisdom, and helps meet the many needs of the creatures spread all over the earth. But it does not reach every place where it is needed on its own; man has to put in some skill and labour to take it where it is required.
- **Air**, by contrast, is a compulsory gift that reaches every place without any labour or active role from human beings. Even someone who wanted to avoid it would have to exert extra labour.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this is not the place to describe Allah's creations and their characteristics, as it would need volumes: each and every creation of Allah is perfect in its purpose and has its own peculiar properties and traits — and Imam Ghazzālī wrote a book on the subject, *al-Ḥikma fī Makhlūqāt Allāh Taʿālā*.

So "measured it exactly" is not a poetic flourish. The point Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is making is one of fit: the ground firm enough to build on and soft enough to dig, water abundant but requiring your effort, air free and unavoidable. Each thing is made to suit the purpose for which it was created — that is what *faqaddarahu taqdīran* is naming.

## Ayah 3: the foolishness of taking other gods

Ayah 3 lands as the verdict on everything ayah 2 established: **"Yet they have taken besides Him other gods who created nothing but are themselves created, and possess neither harm nor benefit for themselves, and possess no power of causing death, nor of giving life, nor of raising the dead."**

Ibn Kathīr heads this section *The Foolishness of the Idolators*, and reads it as Allah telling us of the ignorance of the idolaters in taking other gods instead of Allah — the Creator of all things, the One who controls the affairs of all things, so that whatever He wills happens and whatever He does not will does not happen. In spite of that, they still worshipped others besides Him: idols who **could not even create the wing of a gnat**, but were themselves created.

Follow the logic as he lays it out. These objects could neither do harm nor bring benefit **to themselves** — so how could they do anything for their worshippers? That is the whole question, and it answers itself.

Then the final clause raises the stakes to the only three powers that ultimately matter: **death, life, and resurrection.** Ibn Kathīr: they could not do any of that at all; that power belongs only to Allah, who is the One who gives life and death, and who will bring all people, the first and the last, back to life on the Day of Resurrection.

And to show how effortless that resurrection is for Him, he strings together the ayat that describe it as a single instant:

> *"The creation of you all and the resurrection of you all are only as (the creation and resurrection of) a single person."* (31:28)
> *"And Our commandment is but one, as the twinkling of an eye."* (54:50)
> *"But it will be only a single Zajrah (shout). When behold, they find themselves on the surface of the earth alive after their death."* (79:13–14)
> *"It will be a single Zajrah, and behold, they will be staring!"* (37:19)
> *"It will be but a single Ṣayḥah (cry), so behold they will all be brought up before Us!"* (36:53)

Everything the false gods cannot do at all, Allah does with one word.

## Where the passage lands

Ibn Kathīr closes with a statement of pure tawḥīd, and it is the natural conclusion of the three ayat: He is Allah, besides whom there is no other deity and besides whom there is no other Lord. No one should be worshipped except Him, because whatever He wills happens and whatever He does not will does not happen. He has no offspring nor progenitor, nor equal, nor likeness, nor rival, nor peer. He is the One, the Self-Sufficient Master whom all creatures need; He begets not, nor was He begotten, and there is none co-equal or comparable unto Him.

**Living it.** Read the three ayat as one movement and they leave you with a practical shape:

1. **Begin with praise, not defence.** The disbelievers had raised doubts and objections; the sūrah answers them — but its first word is *tabāraka*, blessing the One who sent the Book down. Confidence in the Qurʼān rests on knowing who spoke it.
2. **Let the Book actually judge.** *Furqān* is the criterion that decides between truth and falsehood, guidance and misguidance, lawful and unlawful. It is only working in your life if it is deciding things for you — including where the verdict is inconvenient.
3. **Take servanthood as the honour it is.** The title Allah gave His Messenger ﷺ at the noblest moments was *His servant*, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says no greater honour exists than being called by Allah "His own."
4. **Read the world as measured.** Every fitted thing around you — earth firm enough to build on and soft enough to dig, air arriving without any labour of yours — is *faqaddarahu taqdīran* in front of your eyes.
5. **Weigh anything you lean on against ayah 3.** Did it create anything? Can it bring benefit or harm to itself? Does it hold death, life, or resurrection? If not, it has no claim on the part of your heart that belongs to Allah alone.

passages.title: The charge that the Quran is fabricated fables
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat put the objections of those who disbelieve on record — that the Qur'an is a forgery, that a team of helpers produced it, that it is nothing but old stories dictated to the Prophet ﷺ each morning and evening — and then answer all of it in a single sentence. What holds the passage together is that shape: three ayat of accusation and reply, where the reply does not argue about the man at all but points to the Source of the Book, and then, astonishingly, ends by offering the accusers forgiveness.

## The three charges

**Ayah 4** carries two of them. First, *"This is nothing but a lie that he has invented."* Ibn Kathir glosses **ifk** (إِفْك) simply as an untruth, and **iftarāhu** — "he has invented it" — as referring to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Second: *"and others have helped him in it"* — which, Ibn Kathir explains, means that he asked other people to help him compile it. So the charge is not merely that he made it up, but that he could not even have made it up alone.

**Ayah 5** sharpens the picture into a specific, almost documentary story: *"Tales of the ancients which he has written down, and they are dictated to him morning and afternoon."* On **asāṭīr al-awwalīn** — "tales of the ancients" — with **iktatabahā**, Ibn Kathir says the meaning is that the ancients wrote these things down and he has copied them. **Tumlā ʿalayhi**, "dictated to him," means they are read or recited to him. And **bukratan wa aṣīlan** means at the beginning and the end of the day.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out the accusation as the objectors themselves framed it: the Qur'an is not a revealed book but a compilation from old stories and narrations of the Jews and Christians, reduced to writing by the Companions — because the Prophet ﷺ was unlettered and could not write. Being unable to read or write, he would have them read out to him day and night until he had them by heart, then repeat them before people and claim they were revelation from Allah.

Notice how much effort went into that theory. It is not the shrug of a man who has not thought about it. It is a whole imagined workflow: sources, scribes, daily dictation, memorisation, performance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that from this point onward the objections raised against the Qur'an and against the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ are related one after another, each together with its answer.

## Allah's verdict on the charge: *an unjust wrong and a lie*

The reply to ayah 4 comes in the same ayah: *"In fact, they have produced an unjust wrong and a lie"* — **ẓulman wa zūran**. Ibn Kathir's comment is worth reading slowly: *they* are the ones telling a lie, and **they know that it is false** — "for their own souls know that what they are claiming is not true."

That is the heart of it. The accusation of forgery is itself the forgery. And the Qur'an's own verdict on it is not that it is a mistaken opinion sincerely held. It is named as a wrong and as a falsehood — told, as Ibn Kathir says, by people whose own souls knew better.

## Why the charge collapsed under its own weight

Ibn Kathir does not merely deny the accusation; he shows why the people who heard it could see through it, and the argument is drawn from the Prophet's ﷺ own life among them.

**He never learned to read or write.** Ibn Kathir says this is known through *Mutawātir* reports and is a common fact: he never learned, neither at the beginning of his life nor at the end of it. This was not a contested point that needed proving; as Ibn Kathir puts it, the idea in ayah 5 is so foolish and so patently false that everyone knows it is not true. The picture of a man poring over copied manuscripts is a picture of somebody who did not exist.

**They had watched him for forty years.** He grew up among them for approximately forty years, from the time he was born until the time his mission began. Ibn Kathir presses this: they knew all about him, about his honest and sound character, and that he would never lie or do anything immoral or bad. They even used to call him **Al-Amīn** — the Trustworthy One — from a young age right up until his mission began, precisely because they saw how truthful and honest he was. The title was theirs, not his; they gave it because the evidence of decades demanded it.

**Then the honour came, and the enmity came with it.** When Allah honoured him with that which He honoured him, Ibn Kathir says, they declared their enmity towards him and came up with all these accusations which any reasonable person would know he was innocent of. And here is the tell: they were not sure what to accuse him of. Sometimes they said he was a sorcerer; at other times a poet, or crazy, or a liar. Ibn Kathir cites the Qur'an's own comment on this thrashing about: *"See what examples they have put forward for you. So they have gone astray, and never can they find a way."* (17:48). A man with the truth does not need four incompatible explanations for the same thing. People who change the charge every week are not following evidence; they are looking for a charge that will stick.

Read this way, ayat 4–5 are not merely reporting slander. Allah is placing their words on permanent record so that every later generation can hold the accusation up against the life of the accused and see the mismatch for themselves.

## Ayah 6: the answer does not defend the man — it names the Sender

*"Say: 'It has been sent down by Him Who knows the secret of the heavens and the earth. Truly, He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.'"*

The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to say **anzalahu** — *He* sent it down. The answer bypasses the biography entirely and rests the case on the Book itself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks what that reply contains. The essence is that the Qur'an is its own evidence that it is the Divine message from Him who is Omniscient and who knows fully well all the secrets of the heavens and the earth. This is why the Qur'an is a miraculous message, and why the whole world is challenged to bring out a sūrah — or even a single ayah — to match it, if its divine origin is refused. And consider who the challenge was addressed to: the Arabs, a people well known for their literary proficiency and art of expression, for whom composing a piece of literature was not a problem. Yet they did not dare attempt it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the contrast unbearable for the objection: these were people willing to sacrifice all their material wealth to oppose his mission, willing to sacrifice even their children and their own lives to counter him — but they dared not attempt to compose a passage similar to a sūrah of the Qur'an.

That is the quiet demolition of ayah 5's theory. If the Qur'an were a scrapbook of borrowed stories written up by helpers, the obvious counter-move was to gather better helpers and produce a better scrapbook. They spent everything except the one thing that would have ended the matter. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes: this is clear proof that it is not the work of a human being — otherwise other people could also have composed passages similar to it.

And it is not only the language. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that apart from the beauty of expression and language, the Book also excels in its **meanings**: the many subjects it covers can only be dealt with by One who knows everything, whether hidden or exposed. Ibn Kathir says the same from the other side: the One who sent it down revealed a Qur'an which includes true information about the earlier and later generations, information which concurs with the realities of the past and future. A collection of "tales of the ancients" would tell you about the past at best. This Book tells you about what is coming.

## "Who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth"

Ibn Kathir explains the phrase: Allah is the One Who knows the unseen in the heavens and on the earth; He knows their secrets just as He knows what is visible therein. We affirm that as it comes — His knowledge reaches the hidden exactly as it reaches the open — without likening it to anything in creation and without explaining it away.

Placed here, that description does two things at once. It establishes the Book's origin: only such a Knower could send down a revelation of this reach. And it turns on the accusers. Ibn Kathir's earlier note — *their own souls know that what they are claiming is not true* — lands on this attribute with full force. The One replying to them is the One who knows secrets: He knows what the accusers privately believed while their mouths said otherwise. He has read the inside of the argument, not just the outside.

## The ending nobody expects: *Ghafūr, Raḥīm*

After an accusation this ugly, the ayah could have closed with a threat. Instead it closes: *"Truly, He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."*

Ibn Kathir reads this as an invitation to them to repent and turn back to Allah, telling them that His mercy is vast and His patience is immense, and that whoever repents to Him, He accepts his repentance. Despite all their lies, immorality, falsehood, disbelief and stubbornness — despite exactly what they had just said about the Messenger ﷺ and about the Qur'an — He still invites them to repent, give up their sin, and come to Islam and true guidance.

He shows this is the Qur'an's habit. After the severe words about those who said "Allah is the third of the three" and the warning of a painful torment, the passage continues: *"Will they not turn with repentance to Allah and ask His forgiveness? For Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."* (5:73–74). And in the ayah about those who put the believing men and women to trial, the door is left visibly open by the words *"and then do not turn in repentance"* — the punishment named is for those who refuse to repent (85:10).

On this, Ibn Kathir quotes Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī, who said: **"Look at this kindness and generosity! They killed His friends and He is calling them to repentance and mercy."**

There is a striking symmetry in the passage. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this sūrah, at its very beginning, addresses the one on whom the Book was revealed as **ʿabduhu**, "His slave" — and that there cannot be a greater honour for anyone than to be called by Allah as 'His own'. So within a few lines: they call him a forger and a copyist; Allah calls him *His slave*. They tell lies about him; Allah offers them forgiveness.

## Living it

**Judge a claim by the life of the one making it.** Ibn Kathir's whole defence is the Prophet's ﷺ record — forty years of it, certified by the very people who later turned against him, with the title Al-Amīn. That is how honest people assess a claim, and it is also a standard we are meant to be measured by: build a life so consistent that slander against you sounds implausible to anyone who knows you.

**Expect the accusations to shift, and don't be shaken.** Sorcerer, poet, crazy, liar — Ibn Kathir points out that they were not sure what to accuse him of. When criticism of Islam or of you keeps changing shape, that instability is itself information.

**Answer from the Book's own weight.** Ayah 6 does not say "look how good he is." It says *"Say: He sent it down."* The strongest answer available to a believer facing this charge is the same one Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives: the Qur'an's language, its knowledge of past and future, and the fact that the challenge to produce its like has never been met.

**Keep the door open for the ones attacking you.** This is the hardest instruction in the passage and the plainest. Allah answered the worst thing they had ever said about His Book by reminding them He forgives. If that is how the accused Messenger ﷺ was told to end his reply, it is not for us to slam doors that Allah has left open.

passages.title: Mocking a messenger who eats and walks markets
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat record the objections the disbelievers of Makkah raised against the Prophet ﷺ — that he ate food, walked in the markets, had no angel beside him, no treasure, no garden — and then Allah's verdict on those objections. What holds the passage together is a single question: what would a true messenger have to look like? They had an answer ready, and Allah's reply in ayah 9 does not debate that answer. It shows where holding it has left them.

## Where this sits in the argument

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that from the previous ayat onward the Qur'an is presenting the objections of the disbelievers **together with their answers**, one after another. The first objection came just before our passage: they claimed the Qur'an was not a revealed book at all but something compiled from the old stories and narrations of the Jews and Christians, written down by the Companions — since the Prophet ﷺ was unlettered and could not write. Because he could not read or write, they said, he would have them read out to him day and night until he had them by heart, and then repeat them before people and claim he had received them from Allah.

That objection was answered in ayah 6: *"Say, 'It is sent down by the One who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth.'"* The Qur'an, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is its own evidence: the Book excels not only in expression and language but in its meanings, and the many subjects it covers could only be handled by One who knows everything, whether hidden or exposed. This is why the whole world is challenged to bring a single sūrah, or even a verse, to match it. That challenge was thrown at the Arabs — a people known for their literary proficiency and art of expression, for whom composing a piece of literature was no difficulty, and a people willing to spend their wealth, their children and their own lives to counter the Prophet ﷺ and his message. Yet, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, they did not dare attempt to compose anything like a sūrah of the Qur'an.

Our passage is the **second objection**. Having failed to explain away the Book, they turned on the man who brought it.

## "He eats food and walks in the markets"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out their reasoning plainly: if he were really a prophet he should not have been eating and drinking like common people; he should have been free of eating and drinking, like the angels. Ibn Kathir catches the sneer in ayah 7 exactly — *(Why does this Messenger eat food)* means "**as we eat** — why does he need food as we need it?"

The second half of the complaint is even more revealing. *Wa yamshī fī l-aswāq* — "and walks about in the markets." Ibn Kathir explains that this means he walks around and goes there often, **seeking to trade and earn a living**. The *sūq* was the ordinary place of buying and selling, of haggling and daily work. So their picture of a messenger was of someone lifted out of ordinary human life: no hunger, no marketplace, no need to earn. The man in front of them was hungry like them and worked like them, and to them that settled the matter.

Notice what has happened. They have taken the two most universal facts of human existence — you must eat, and you must work — and turned them into disqualifications. Ibn Kathir opens his commentary on this passage by saying that Allah is telling us here about the disbelievers' **stubborn resistance to and rejection of the truth, with no proof or evidence for doing so**. That phrase is the key to the whole passage: what looks like an argument is only a refusal wearing the clothes of an argument.

## The three things they demanded instead

Having said what a messenger should not be, they list what he should have had.

**An angel sent down with him.** In ayah 7: *"Why is not an angel sent down to him to be a warner with him?"* Ibn Kathir explains their meaning — why does an angel not come down to him from Allah **to be a witness that what he is claiming is true**? Not an angel to warn them; an angel to authenticate him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point: how could he be accepted as a prophet when he is neither an angel himself, nor does an angel accompany him to endorse what he preaches?

**A treasure.** In ayah 8: *"or a treasure had been cast down to him."* Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: treasure that **he could spend on his needs and wants**.

**A garden.** *"or he had had a garden"* to eat from. Here Ibn Kathir gives a striking gloss: they wanted **a garden that would go with him wherever he went**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the thinking behind both demands: failing his being an angel, he should at least have had enough wealth and gardens to take care of his day-to-day needs, **so that he may not need to care for his living**. That is the point of the two demands taken together — a messenger, in their eyes, should have been visibly exempt from the business of making a living.

Then comes the sentence that a believer should sit with. All of this, Ibn Kathir says, **is easy for Allah** — the angel, the treasure, the garden; none of it strains His power for a moment. He simply did not do it: "He had a reason for not doing any of these things, and with Him is the perfect proof and argument." Notice what Ibn Kathir does not say. He does not tell us what that reason was. Their demands were not refused because they were too much to ask; they were refused for a reason that belongs to Allah, and the tafsir leaves it exactly there, with the perfect proof and argument resting with Him.

## The same script Firʿawn used

Ibn Kathir draws a line from Makkah back to Egypt. Firʿawn said of Mūsā, peace be upon him: *"Why then are not golden bracelets bestowed on him, or angels sent along with him?"* (43:53). Gold and angels — the identical pair. "These people," Ibn Kathir writes, "had a similar mentality and said the same kind of thing."

It is worth pausing on that. Centuries apart, in different languages, opposing different prophets, rejection reaches for the same two props: visible wealth, and a supernatural escort. The objection is not really about evidence. It is about a settled instinct that truth ought to arrive dressed in power, and a refusal to accept it when it arrives dressed as a working man.

## "You follow none but a man bewitched"

The final move in ayah 8 is directed not at the Prophet ﷺ but at the people listening to him: *"You follow none but a man bewitched."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the logic: since he is neither an angel nor has an angel with him, **it appears that he has been charmed by someone which has turned his head, and that is why he talks like this**. In other words: he is not lying to you, he is not himself. It is the kindest-sounding of all their accusations and the most corrosive, because it asks his followers to pity him rather than listen to him.

Note whom Allah names as the speakers: *wa qāla ẓ-ẓālimūn* — **"and the wrongdoers said."** Not "and they said." The verdict on the speakers is delivered inside the report of their speech.

## Allah's answer: "See how they coin similitudes for you"

Ayah 9 is the turn: *"See how they coin similitudes for you, so they have gone astray, and they cannot find a path."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this **the general answer** to the whole objection; the detailed answers are given in the next few ayat. Before Allah takes their claims apart one by one, He first shows His Prophet ﷺ what those claims are.

*Amthāl* here means the comparisons and labels they coined for him. Ibn Kathir explains: they accused you and belied you when they said that you were a **sorcerer**, or **bewitched**, or **crazy**, or a **liar**, or a **poet** — "but all of these are false ideas. Everyone who has the slightest understanding will recognise that they are lying."

Notice how Ibn Kathir handles that list. He does not rank the labels, and he does not take them up one at a time to refute each in turn. He sets them all aside together, in one sentence, as false ideas that anyone with the slightest understanding can see through.

**"So they have gone astray"** — Ibn Kathir: astray from the path of guidance. This is the answer to the mockery, and it is not a counter-insult. Allah does not argue their labels down. He simply reports where their labelling has landed them.

## "And they cannot find a path"

Ibn Kathir's comment on the closing words of ayah 9 is one of the most useful sentences in this passage:

> Everyone who steps outside of the way of truth and guidance has gone astray, **no matter what direction he takes**, because the truth is one and its methodology is unified, parts of it confirming other parts.

Truth is not one option among many. There is one road, and every step off it is a step away, whichever way it points. That is why a person who has left guidance can generate objection after objection — sorcerer, poet, madman — and still get nowhere: he is not moving toward anything.

For the Prophet ﷺ, who was being mocked in his own city by his own people, there is a mercy folded into this. The command is *unẓur* — "look, see." Look at what they are reduced to. Their words tell you about them, not about you.

## *Tabāraka* — the answer that redraws the picture

Ayah 10 answers the demand for treasure and gardens without conceding a single inch of its premise: *"Blessed is the One Who — if He wills — can give you far better than that: gardens under which rivers flow, and will assign you palaces."*

Ibn Kathir introduces it exactly so: Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ that if He willed, He **could** bestow on him in this world something far better than what they were saying. Mujahid said of "better than that": **"This means in this world."** And Mujahid adds a detail that lets you hear the ayah as its first audience heard it: the Quraysh **used to call every house that was made of stone a "palace," whether it was large or small**.

That detail is quietly devastating. The people demanding a treasure and a garden as the price of belief were people for whom a modest stone house counted as a palace. Their imagination of grandeur was small. And Allah's reply is not "he does not need those things"; it is that the One being mocked through him could hand him gardens with rivers running beneath them and palaces besides. Why He did not, Ibn Kathir has already told us as much as we are told: all of this is easy for Allah, but He had a reason for not doing any of these things — a reason He keeps, and with Him is the perfect proof and argument.

Two things are being affirmed here at once, and mainstream Sunni belief holds both without compromise: Allah's power is complete — nothing they proposed is beyond Him — and Allah's will is free — He gives and withholds as He chooses, not according to what the objectors think would look right. *In shāʼa* ("if He wills") is the hinge of the ayah; the whole reply hangs on His will, not on their expectations.

## What the passage exposes next

Ibn Kathir carries the thread into the ayah that follows our range: *"Nay, they deny the Hour."* This, he says, means they say this **in stubborn disbelief, not because they are seeking insight and guidance** — it is their disbelief in the Day of Resurrection that makes them say what they say. That is the diagnosis behind the whole passage. The complaints about food, markets, angels, treasure and gardens were never the disease. A man who genuinely expects to stand before Allah does not measure a messenger by his shopping.

## Living it

**Honest work is not beneath the sacred.** Their charge was that he walked the markets seeking to trade and earn a living, and Allah never denies it — the objection is answered without the fact being disowned. A believer earning his bread in the marketplace stands in a line the Messenger ﷺ himself walked.

**Wealth is not a certificate of truth.** The demand for a treasure and a garden, and Firʿawn's demand for golden bracelets before it, are the same error dressed for different centuries: assuming that if it were really from Allah, it would be visibly rich. Ayah 10 answers by pointing out how easily Allah could have supplied it — and did not.

**Test claims by evidence, not by packaging.** Ibn Kathir's opening charge against them is that they resisted the truth **with no proof or evidence**. Anyone can dress a preference up as an objection. The honest question is always: what is my actual evidence, and would I accept this reasoning if it pointed the other way?

**When you are mocked for your religion, look at what the mockery is made of.** Sorcerer, bewitched, crazy, liar, poet — and, as Ibn Kathir says, all of them false ideas that anyone with the slightest understanding can see through. Ayah 9 does not tell the Prophet ﷺ to answer them. It tells him to *see* them, and leaves their condition — astray, unable to find a path — as the whole reply.

passages.title: Denial of the Hour: the Blaze versus the Garden
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

The Makkans had been picking at the Prophet ﷺ with objections — why does he eat food, why does he walk about in the markets, why is no angel sent down with him as a warner, why has he no treasure or garden to eat from (ayat 7–8)? Ayat 11–16 answer by exposing the real motive underneath the questions, and then by putting the two possible endings of a human life side by side: a Fire that has already been prepared, and a Garden that has already been promised. What holds these six ayat together is that single contrast, ending in the question of ayah 15 — *is that better, or this?*

## "Nay" — the objections were never the point

*"Nay, they deny the Hour."* Ibn Kathir reads the shift precisely. All those objections, he says, were said "in stubborn disbelief, not because they are seeking insight and guidance, but because their disbelief in the Day of Resurrection makes them say what they say."

That is the passage's first and deepest lesson. The stated objection is rarely the real one. A man who genuinely wanted to know whether Muhammad ﷺ was a Messenger could weigh the evidence; Ibn Kathir notes that the charges thrown at him — sorcerer, bewitched, crazy, liar, poet — are "all of these are false ideas," and "everyone who has the slightest understanding will recognize that they are lying." They were not weighing anything. They had already decided there would be no Hour, and every objection after that was decoration on a conclusion already reached.

Ibn Kathir also observes that this mentality is old. Of the demand for an angel he says it "is like when Fir'awn said: *'Why then are not golden bracelets bestowed on him, or angels sent along with him?'*" (43:53) — and he comments that "these people had a similar mentality and said the same kind of thing." Gold and an escorting angel: the same demand, made again generations later.

And on the demands themselves Ibn Kathir is careful to say that "all of this is easy for Allah, but He had a reason for not doing any of these things, and with Him is the perfect proof and argument." Allah does not decline the demand out of inability; His wisdom decides what a Messenger is given. Indeed ayah 10 has just said that He could assign His Prophet gardens and palaces if He willed — Mujahid explains this to mean **in this world** — and Mujahid adds the homely detail that the Quraysh "used to call every house that was made of stone a 'palace', whether it was large or small." The thing they thought so grand was, by their own usage, a stone house.

## Already made ready

**وَأَعْتَدْنَا** — "and We have prepared". Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: "We have made ready." The verb is past tense. The Fire is not a threat that will be constructed if people persist; it is a place already furnished and waiting, while the deniers are still busy denying. And notice how exactly the punishment fits: it is prepared **for the one who denied the Hour**. The very thing they said did not exist is what receives them.

Of the words rendered "a flaming Fire," Ibn Kathir says they mean "an unbearably hot and painful torment in the fire of Hell."

## A fire that sees, rages, and roars (ayah 12)

Here the Qur'an does something startling. It gives the Fire a face.

*"When it sees them from a far place, they will hear its raging and its roaring."* Ibn Kathir explains the words directly: "when Hell sees them" — and "from a far place" means "from the place of gathering (on the Day of Resurrection)." So before the condemned ever reach it, it has already caught sight of them across that vast plain.

Then the sound. Of *"they will hear its raging and its roaring,"* Ibn Kathir says: "(it will make those sounds) out of hatred towards them." This is not machinery. It is personal. He brings the parallel from Sūrat al-Mulk: *"When they are cast therein, they will hear the terrible drawing in of its breath as it blazes forth. It almost bursts up with fury"* (67:7–8) — which, he says, means that parts of it almost separate from other parts "because of its intense hatred towards those who disbelieved in Allah."

This belongs to the matters of the unseen, which we receive as they came. The Qur'an tells us the Fire sees and rages; we affirm what Allah has said without picturing it in terms of the creatures we know, and without emptying the words of their meaning.

**Two reports Ibn Kathir brings here.** Imam Abu Ja'far bin Jarir narrated that Ibn 'Abbas said — and Ibn Kathir adds, *"Its chain of narrators is Sahih"* — that a man will be dragged towards Hell, which will be expanding and contracting, and Ar-Rahman will say to it, *"What is the matter with you?"* It will say, *"He is seeking refuge from me."* So Allah will say, *"Let My servant go."* Another man will be dragged towards Hell and will say, *"O Lord, I never expected this from You."* Allah will say, *"What did you expect?"* The man will say, *"I expected that Your mercy would be great enough to include me."* So Allah will say, *"Let My servant go."* Another man will be dragged towards Hell, and Hell will bray at him like a donkey braying at barley; then it will give a moan that will instil fear in everyone.

Sit with the middle of that. In the most terrifying place imaginable, two things save two men: seeking refuge from the Fire, and expecting Allah's mercy to be wide enough to include them. And the name used in the report is **Ar-Rahman** — the Most Merciful — precisely there, at the mouth of the Fire. The same passage that prepares a blaze for the deniers records Allah releasing servants who turned to Him.

The second report: 'Abdur-Razzaq recorded that 'Ubayd bin 'Umayr said, *"Hell will utter a moan such that there will be no angel who is close to Allah and no Prophet sent to mankind, but he will fall on his face, shaking all over. Even Ibrahim, peace be upon him, will fall to his knees and say: 'O Lord, I do not ask You for salvation this Day except for myself.'"* If that sound brings the closest angels and the greatest Prophets to the ground, no one should be casual about that Day.

## Narrow, chained, crying ruin (ayat 13–14)

Ayah 13 concentrates the torment into three details, and each one removes a form of relief.

**A narrow place.** Qatadah narrated from Abu Ayyub that 'Abdullah bin 'Amr said of it: "Like the point of a spear, i.e., in its narrowness." Hell is vast, yet what is given to them within it is a constricted space. Part of what makes suffering bearable in this life is room: room to shift, to turn away, to breathe. That is taken first.

**مُّقَرَّنِينَ** — "chained together". Abu Salih said, "This means, tied from their shoulders." Bound at the shoulder, arms fixed. Ibn Kathir sums up the whole condition in his comment on ayah 15: they are "unable to move or call for help, and unable to escape their plight."

**"They will exclaim therein for destruction."** Ibn Kathir says this means "they will utter cries of woe, regret and sorrow." This is what is left when a human being has no action available at all — only a voice.

And then ayah 14 takes even that away: *"Exclaim not today for one destruction, but exclaim for many destructions."* It sounds like an answer, but it grants nothing. The cry asks for an end; the reply refuses to give one, and multiplies the cry instead. There is no exit at the end of the screaming.

## The question that ends the argument (ayah 15)

Then the tone changes completely. *"Say: Is that better, or the Paradise of Eternity which is promised to those who have Taqwa?"*

Ibn Kathir paraphrases its force. Allah is saying: 'O Muhammad, this that We have described to you about the state of those who are doomed, who will be dragged on their faces to Hell, "which will receive them with a scowling face, with hatred and moans," thrown into their constricted spaces, tied up to their shoulders, "unable to move or call for help, and unable to escape their plight — is this better, or the eternal Paradise which Allah has promised to the pious among His servants, which He has prepared for them as a reward and ultimate destiny in return for their obedience to Him in this world?"'

Notice that the Prophet ﷺ is told **قُلْ** — *say*. He is not asked to invent a new argument; he is handed a question to put to them. And it is a question no one can get wrong. That is exactly the point: the people demanding treasure and gardens *in this life* are being shown what they are trading away. The Qur'an does not shout them down. It lays the two endings next to each other and asks them to choose.

Note the wording of the reward, too: it is promised to **ٱلۡمُتَّقُونَ** (*al-muttaqūn*), those who have *taqwā* — Ibn Kathir renders them "the pious among His servants," those who guard themselves in awareness of Allah. And he describes the Garden as theirs "as a reward and ultimate destiny in return for their obedience to Him in this world." The Garden answers a life, not a wish.

Ibn Kathir also points out a pattern in how Allah teaches. "In this Surah Allah mentions Hell, then refers to the situation of the people of Paradise." In Sūrat as-Sāffāt the order is reversed: there Allah mentions the people of Paradise "with its beauty and joy," and then asks, *"Is that better entertainment or the tree of Zaqqūm?"* (37:62–70). Either way the method is the same — the two destinations are set side by side so the mind can weigh them.

## Whatever they wish, forever, and a promise that must come to pass (ayah 16)

Three phrases, each answering something in the Fire.

**"For them there will be therein all that they desire."** Against the narrow place and the chains — total freedom of desire. Ibn Kathir lists what he can: delights "such as food, drink, clothing, dwellings, means of transportation and scenery" — and then language runs out, and he adds "other things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, nor the heart of anyone can comprehend." In the Fire they had one thing left, a cry, and it was refused. In the Garden, whatever they wish is granted.

**خَالِدِينَ — "abiding forever."** Ibn Kathir: "They will abide therein forever; it will never cease or come to an end, and they will never leave it." The Garden of *al-khuld* — the Garden of Eternity — is named in ayah 15 for exactly this. Every joy in this world is shadowed by its ending; that shadow is removed.

**كَانَ عَلَىٰ رَبِّكَ وَعْدًا مَّسْئُولًا** — "it is upon your Lord a *wa'dan mas'ūlā*." Ibn Kathir explains that this means "it must inevitably come to pass," and reports that Abu Ja'far bin Jarir related from some of the scholars of the Arabic language that *wa'dan mas'ūlā* means **a binding pledge**. Sit with the wording: **عَلَىٰ رَبِّكَ**, *upon your Lord*. The Fire is **prepared**; the Garden is **pledged**. Both are settled before the Day ever arrives.

## Living it

**Check your real objection.** Ayah 11 says the questions were never the problem — the denial of the Hour was. When we find ourselves arguing with a command of Allah, the honest question is whether we have a genuine difficulty or whether the Hour has simply gone dim in the heart. Belief in the Day of Resurrection is the root that keeps everything else upright.

**Do not be casual about the Fire.** In the report from 'Ubayd bin 'Umayr, its moan brings the closest angels and the Prophets to the ground. Allah tells us what has been prepared so that we take it seriously now, while taking it seriously still changes something.

**Seek refuge, and expect His mercy.** In the report from Ibn 'Abbas whose chain Ibn Kathir called Sahih, two men were released at the very edge — one because he was seeking refuge from the Fire, one because he expected Allah's mercy to be great enough to include him. Both are habits a believer can build today: asking Allah for protection from the Fire, and never letting fear collapse into despair of His mercy.

**Live toward what is promised.** Ibn Kathir describes Paradise as prepared for the pious "in return for their obedience to Him in this world," and the promise of it as something that "must inevitably come to pass." It is not in doubt; what is in doubt is us. So the question of ayah 15 is not rhetorical for the one who hears it — it is a choice to be lived out, today, in obedience.

passages.title: False gods disown their worshippers on Judgement Day
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat show us a single scene on the Day of Resurrection: Allah gathers the idolaters together with the very beings they worshipped instead of Him, questions those worshipped beings, and lets the worshippers hear themselves disowned. The Tafsir Ibn Kathir material on this passage carries the heading *The gods of the Idolators Will Disown Them on the Day of Resurrection*. Ayah 17 sets the scene and puts the question; ayah 18 gives the answer of those who were worshipped; ayah 19 turns from them to the worshippers with the verdict.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this part of Sūrat al-Furqān is working through the objections the deniers raised against the Prophet ﷺ. Their second objection was that a real prophet should not eat and drink like common people — he should have been free of that, like angels; or failing that, he should at least have had enough wealth and gardens to take care of his day-to-day needs, so that he need not worry about his living. And how could he be accepted as a prophet, they said, when he is neither an angel nor has an angel accompanying him to endorse what he preaches? So, they concluded, someone must have charmed him and turned his head, and that is why he talks this way. The general answer to this objection, Maʿārif notes, is the ayah *See how they coined similes for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way* (25:9), with the detailed answer given in the next few verses.

Keep that in mind and the force of our passage becomes sharper. These people set the bar of "real religion" at angels — and here Allah shows them the Day when the angels themselves stand before Him and say it was never right for them to be taken as protectors besides Him.

## Ayah 17: the gathering, and the question

**"And on the Day when He will gather them together and that which they worship besides Allah."** Ibn Kathir opens the passage by saying that Allah is telling us what will happen on the Day of Resurrection, when those whom the idolaters used to worship instead of Allah — angels and others — will rebuke them. What makes this gathering so heavy is who is gathered with whom: the worshippers are brought together with the objects of their worship.

Who are these worshipped beings? Mujahid said: **"This means ʿĪsā, ʿUzayr and the angels."** So the beings in question here are themselves servants of Allah, raised by their worshippers into a place they never asked for.

Then comes the question. **"He will say: 'Was it you who misled these My servants, or did they stray from the path?'"** Ibn Kathir renders Allah's meaning as: Allah will say to those who were worshipped, *Did you call these people to worship you instead of Me, or was it their own idea to worship you, without any call to that on your part?*

Ibn Kathir points to the closest parallel in the Qurʼān, where Allah says to ʿĪsā, *"O ʿĪsā, son of Maryam! Did you say unto men: 'Worship me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'"* and ʿĪsā answers, *"Glory be to You! It was not for me to say what I had no right to say. Had I said such a thing, You would surely have known it. You know what is in my innerself though I do not know what is in Yours; truly, You, only You, are the All-Knower of all that is hidden. Never did I say to them aught except what You did command me to say"* (5:116–117). Our passage is the same courtroom, widened to include the others who were worshipped.

## Ayah 18: "Glorified be You!"

Their reply does not begin with self-defence. It begins with **Subḥānaka — rendered "Glorified be You!"** Before they clear their own names, they exalt Allah. That is exactly how ʿĪsā's answer begins in the ayah Ibn Kathir has just quoted (*"Glory be to You!"*), and exactly how the angels answer in the other parallel he cites: *"And remember the Day when He will gather them all together, then He will say to the angels: 'Was it you that these people used to worship?' They (the angels) will say: 'Glorified be You!'"* (34:40–41). Three separate scenes, one reflex.

**"It was not for us to take any awliyāʼ besides You."** Ibn Kathir glosses *awliyāʼ* as **protectors or helpers** — and that is precisely the relationship the idolaters had constructed.

Ibn Kathir notes a point of recitation here: **most of the scholars recite a fatḥah on the nūn of the word *nattakhidh*** in *nattakhidha min dūnika min awliyāʼ*. On that reading the sense is, as he puts it: *it is not right for any created being, neither us nor them, to worship anyone except You; we did not call them to do that, but they did it of their own accord, without us telling them to do it or accepting what they did. We are innocent of them and their worship.*

Other scholars, he says, understand the phrase to mean: *it is not proper for us to take anyone except You as protectors or helpers (awliyāʼ)* — meaning, *it is not proper for anyone to worship us, for we are Your servants and in need of You.* Ibn Kathir adds that **this meaning is close to the first**. Either way, the confession is the same: those who were worshipped place themselves on the side of servanthood and need.

## "But You gave them comfort" — how it actually happened

If the worshipped ones did not mislead them, what did? Their answer names the cause: **"but You gave them and their fathers comfort till they forgot the Reminder, and became a lost people."**

Of *mattaʿtahum wa ābāʼahum* — **"but You gave them and their fathers comfort"** — Ibn Kathir says the meaning is: *You made such a long period of time pass that they forgot the Reminder*, that is, *they forgot what had been sent down to them through the Messengers, calling them to worship You alone with no partner or associate.*

So on this explanation the ruin did not come through an argument or a seducer. It came through comfort and a long stretch of time, until what the Messengers had brought was simply forgotten. And note that the ayah spans generations: **"them and their fathers."**

**"And became a lost people" — *wa kānū qawman būrā*.** Ibn ʿAbbās said this means **"they were destroyed."** Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Mālik narrated from az-Zuhrī: **"There was no good in them."** Put the two reports together and the picture is of a people with no good left in them, and destroyed.

## Ayah 19: the verdict turns to the worshippers

Now the address swings round. Until here we were listening to Allah and to those who were worshipped; ayah 19 speaks to the idolaters themselves.

**"Thus they have denied you in what you say."** Ibn Kathir explains: *those whom you used to worship besides Allah will show you to be liars in your claims that they were your helpers and protectors bringing you closer to Allah.* The whole justification of their worship is contradicted in public by the very beings it was built on. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel: *And who is more astray than one who calls on besides Allah, such as will not answer him till the Day of Resurrection, and who are unaware of their calls to them. And when mankind are gathered, they will become their enemies and will deny their worshipping* (46:5–6). Not neutral, not merely silent — *enemies*.

**"Then you can neither avert nor find help."** Ibn Kathir's explanation is short and final: *they will not be able to avert the punishment from themselves, nor will they be able to help themselves.* Both doors close at once.

**"And whoever among you does wrong, We shall make him taste a great torment."** Here Ibn Kathir is explicit about what "does wrong" (*yaẓlim*) means in this context: **"by associating others in worship with Allah."** So the "great torment" promised at the end of the passage is not a general threat against sin in the abstract; it is the outcome of the one sin this whole scene has been exposing — giving to a creature the worship that belongs to Allah alone.

## Living it

**Look where your reliance actually rests.** The word in ayah 18 is *awliyāʼ*, which Ibn Kathir glosses as protectors or helpers. That is what the idolaters had made of these beings — they claimed, in Ibn Kathir's words, that they were "your helpers and protectors bringing you closer to Allah." On that Day the claim is publicly denied by the very ones it was made about. Ask honestly what you turn to first when you are afraid.

**Do not let ease do to you what it did to them.** The ayah does not say they were argued out of tawḥīd — the worship of Allah alone with no partner or associate. It says they were given comfort, and a long period passed, until they forgot the Reminder. The antidote is in the diagnosis: keep the Reminder in circulation — recite it, study it, speak it in the house — so that no generation of yours has to receive it half-remembered.

**Honour the righteous without worshipping them.** Mujahid's list — ʿĪsā, ʿUzayr, the angels. On the second explanation Ibn Kathir reports, their own words on that Day are that it is not proper for anyone to worship them, "for we are Your servants and in need of You." Directing worship to them was never something they invited; Ibn Kathir's first explanation has them say plainly, "We are innocent of them and their worship."

**Nothing taken besides Allah will avert or help.** Whatever a person leans on besides Him — a shrine, a saint, a talisman, a system, a self-image — will, on the showing of these ayat, neither turn the punishment aside nor come to the rescue. Better to discover that now, while there is still time to attach oneself to Allah alone.

passages.title: Arrogance demands angels and ends in scattered dust
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat answer an objection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells us that the infidels and polytheists had raised doubts about the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ. Alongside that stands the demand of ayah 21: that angels be sent down where they can be seen. Allah replies on both counts: every messenger sent before him ﷺ was exactly such a man (ayah 20), and the angels being demanded will indeed be seen — on a Day that will bring the criminals no good news at all (ayah 22).

What binds the passage together is a single reversal. Greatness is assumed to be visible: wealth, angels sent down before your eyes, a Lord you can see. Allah shows that the arrangement of the visible world is deliberately a **test** (ayah 20), that the pride behind the demand is itself the disease (ayah 21), that the deeds they were counting on will be scattered like floating dust (ayah 23) — while the dwellers of Paradise will have the best abode and the fairest place of rest (ayah 24).

## The objection behind ayah 20

The objection had two prongs. First: if he were truly a prophet, he would own a great deal of material wealth and gardens and be free from making efforts for his sustenance. Second: a real prophet would not eat and drink like ordinary people nor walk in the markets to earn a livelihood — behind which lay the assumption held by many of them that Allah's messengers could only be angels, never human beings.

To the first, Maʿārif answers that there is no problem for Allah in providing material wealth to His messengers — He could make them kings of mammoth empires, as He did with Sayyidunā Dāwūd and Sayyidunā Sulaymān (peace be upon them), endowed with enormous wealth, itself a clear sign of His omnipotence. But in the interest of common people, and for numerous other considerations, it is required that prophets be kept away from the material wealth of the world. In the case of the Prophet ﷺ specifically, Allah preferred to keep him in line with ordinary Muslims in worldly possessions — and he ﷺ preferred that for himself too.

It is reported in the *Musnad* of Ahmad and in *Tirmidhi*, on the authority of Sayyidunā Abū ʿUmāmah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said Allah offered to turn the entire valley and hills of Makkah into gold for him, and he requested of Him: "No, my Lord — I would prefer that I get sustenance one day (to offer my thanks to You) and go without food the next (to be patient)." And Sayyidah ʿĀʼishah (may Allah be pleased with her) reported that he ﷺ said, "If I wanted, mountains of gold would have been around me" (Mazharī). Ibn Kathīr adds that it is recorded in the Sahih that he ﷺ was given the choice between being a prophet and king, or being a servant and Messenger, and he chose to be a servant and Messenger.

As Maʿārif sums it up: it is Allah's wisdom to keep the prophets poor. And they are not *forced* into that life — Allah has made them such that they do not desire material wealth and instead prefer a simple life.

To the second prong, ayah 20 makes the argument the objectors could not escape: **"And We never sent before you any of the Messengers but verily, they ate food and walked in the markets."** Ibn Kathīr writes that the earlier messengers ate food because their bodies needed the nourishment in it, and went around in the marketplaces seeking to engage in trade and earn a livelihood — and that none of this should affect their status as messengers, because Allah gave them good characteristics, caused them to speak fine words and do noble deeds, and gave them miracles and clear proofs, from which any person of sound insight may see that what they brought from Allah was true. As Maʿārif puts the same argument: the prophets whom the objectors themselves admitted to be prophets were humans too, who ate, drank and worked like ordinary people.

## "We have made some of you a trial for others"

The second half of ayah 20: **"And We have made some of you as a trial for others; will you have patience? And your Lord is Ever All-Seer."**

The word is *fitnah* — a test, a sifting. Ibn Kathīr paraphrases: "We test some of you by means of others, so that We may see who will be obedient and who will be disobedient." Muhammad bin Isḥāq put Allah's meaning like this: "If I had willed that the world be such that no one would oppose My Messengers, I could have made it so, but I wanted to test My servants by means of them." In *Sahih Muslim* it is narrated from ʿIyāḍ bin Ḥimār that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah says: **"I will test you and test others by means of you."**

Then **"will you have patience?"** — a question, not a statement. And **"your Lord is Ever All-Seer"** — Ibn Kathīr explains this as: He knows who deserves to receive revelation, as Allah says elsewhere, *"Allah knows best with whom to place His Message"* (6:124); and He knows who deserves to be guided to the Message with which He sent them, and who does not.

**The wisdom in inequality.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the general principle. Allah had complete power to make all humans wealthy, prosperous, healthy and of high status — but then nobody would have been poor, weak or sick, a position which would have created innumerable social problems resulting in chaos and confusion. So He made some rich and some poor, some healthy and some sick, some strong and some weak, some of high status and some others unknown. This way every single individual is at test because of his or her particular placing in society: **the rich and healthy are at test for their thankfulness, while the poor and sick are on trial for their patience.**

For this very reason, Maʿārif notes, the Prophet ﷺ advised that whenever you see someone wealthier, healthier, stronger or higher in status than you, turn at once toward those who are lower than you in wealth, health, strength and status — so that instead of feeling jealous, which is a sin, you thank Allah for the placing He has given you (Bukhari, Muslim, Mazharī).

## Ayah 21: the people who are not expecting to meet Him

**"And those who expect not a meeting with Us said: 'Why are not the angels sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?'"**

Maʿārif pauses on the word *rajāʼ*. It normally means to hope for something desired; but as Ibn al-Anbārī, the famous scholar of Arabic lexicon, mentioned, it is sometimes used for fear — and that is its sense here. So the phrase means: *those who are not apprehensive of being brought before Us*. The allusion is toward those who totally deny the Hereafter, because only such people could have the courage to put such a frivolous demand. Those who believe in the Hereafter dread it so much that they have no time to waste over such ideas. Maʿārif applies this to its own day: those who appear unsure about the teachings of Islam and indulge in dubious debate under the influence of modern education are showing the weakness of their faith in the Hereafter.

"Why are not the angels sent down to us" means: so that we may see them with our own eyes and they may tell us that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. It is like their other demand, *"or you bring Allah and the angels before us face to face"* (17:92). Allah's own verdict on them follows immediately: **"Indeed they think too highly of themselves, and are scornful with great pride."** Ibn Kathīr sets beside it Allah's words, *"And even if We had sent down unto them angels, and the dead had spoken unto them…"* (6:111).

## Ayah 22: the angels do come

**"On the Day they will see the angels — no good news will there be for the criminals that day."**

Angels were demanded; angels will be seen. Ibn Kathīr notes that this "Day" was located in two places, and then reconciles them:

- **The time of dying.** Ibn Kathīr says this is also confirmed at the time when they are dying, when the angels bring them the tidings of Hell and the wrath of the Compeller. As the disbeliever's soul is being taken out, the angels say to it, "Come out, O evil soul from an evil body, come out to fierce hot wind and boiling water, and the shadow of black smoke." It refuses to come out and scatters throughout his body, so they beat him — as Allah says, *"And if you could see when the angels take away the souls of those who disbelieve; they smite their faces and their backs"* (8:50), and *"And if you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, while the angels are stretching forth their hands… 'Deliver your souls! This day you shall be recompensed with the torment of degradation because of what you used to utter against Allah other than the truth, and you used to reject His Ayat with disrespect!'"* (6:93).
- **The Day of Resurrection.** Other scholars said the ayah refers to the Day of Resurrection. This was the view of Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others.

Ibn Kathīr concludes there is no contradiction between the two views: on both of these days the angels will appear to believers and disbelievers, giving glad tidings of divine mercy and pleasure to the believers, while giving the disbelievers news that will bring regret and sorrow.

For the believer, the same event is pure comfort: *"Verily, those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then they stand firm — on them the angels will descend, saying: 'Fear not, nor grieve! But receive the good news of Paradise which you have been promised.'"* (41:30–32). Ibn Kathīr also cites an authentic hadith narrated from al-Barāʼ bin ʿĀzib: the angels say to the believer's soul at the time of death, "Come out, O good soul in a good body, as you were dwelling in it. Come out to rest and pleasant fragrances and a Lord Who is not angry."

## *Ḥijran maḥjūrā* — a barrier, barred

The ayah ends with a strange, clipped phrase: **wa yaqūlūna ḥijran maḥjūrā**.

**The root.** Ibn Kathīr explains that the basic meaning of *al-ḥijr* is preventing or prohibition. The word is used when a judge prohibits someone — forbidding him to dispose of his wealth in cases of bankruptcy, folly, or being underage. The name of *al-Ḥijr*, the low semicircular wall near the Kaʿbah, is also derived from this root, because it prevents people from making ṭawāf inside it. The mind, too, is called *al-ḥijr*, because it prevents a person from indulging in things that do not befit him. Maʿārif adds a nearer sense: the literal meaning of *ḥijr* is protection, and *maḥjūr* is fully protected — and the Arabs used the expression when danger was in sight, as a way of asking for protection against it.

**Who speaks it.** Ibn Kathīr concludes that the pronoun in "and they will say" refers to **the angels** — they will say to the disbelievers: *success is forbidden to you this day.* This was the view of Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, ʿAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī, Khuṣayf and others, and it was the view favoured by Ibn Jarīr. Ibn Jarīr also recorded that Ibn Jurayj said the words are those of **the idolaters** — that they will seek refuge from the angels, since this is what the Arabs would say when disaster and hardship struck. Ibn Kathīr acknowledges there is a point to what Ibn Jurayj said, but holds that from the context it is unlikely, and that the majority of scholars said something different.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān brings the two readings together in one scene: on that Day, when the disbelievers see the angels approaching them with chastisement, they will utter this word as was their habit in this world, seeking protection — and Sayyidunā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) explained the phrase as *ḥarāman muḥarraman*, banned and prohibited. On that reading, they will plead to be let into Paradise, and the angels will reply with these very words: Paradise is banned and prohibited to them (Mazharī).

## Ayah 23: the deeds they counted on, turned to dust

**"And We shall turn to whatever deeds they did, and We shall make such deeds as scattered floating particles of dust."**

Ibn Kathīr says this refers to the Day of Resurrection, when Allah will bring mankind to account for their deeds, good and bad alike. The deeds these idolaters thought would bring them salvation will be of no avail to them. A deed is futile unless it is both sincere and in accordance with the Laws Allah set out. The deeds of the disbelievers, he says, are lacking in one or the other, or may include both failings, in which case they are even less likely to be accepted.

Then the image itself: *habāʼan manthūrā*. The early authorities reached for different everyday sights, each of something you can see but never hold:

- ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) — narrated by Sufyān ath-Thawrī from Abū Isḥāq from al-Ḥārith — said it is **"the rays of the sun when they pass through a small aperture."** Something similar was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, as-Suddī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: "This refers to the rays coming through a small window, and if anyone tries to grasp them, he cannot."
- ʿAlī is also reported to have said that *habāʼ* refers to **the dust raised by animals** — a similar view coming from Ibn ʿAbbās and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, and also said by ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam.
- Qatādah: "Have you not seen dry trees when they are blown by the wind? This refers to those leaves."
- Yaʿlā bin ʿUbayd: **"Ashes or dust when it is stirred up by the wind."**

All of these views, Ibn Kathīr concludes, point to the same thing: the deeds of the disbelievers will be like some worthless scattered thing. He sets alongside it the Qur'an's other images of the same truth — works that are *"as ashes, on which the wind blows furiously"* (14:18); *"They are not able to do anything with what they have earned"* (2:264); and deeds *"like a mirage in a desert — the thirsty one thinks it to be water, until he comes up to it, he finds it to be nothing"* (24:39).

## Ayah 24: the best abode, the fairest place to rest

**"The dwellers of Paradise will, on that Day, have the best abode, and have the fairest of places for repose."**

After the dust, a place to lie down. Ibn Kathīr reads this as the Day of Resurrection, and as a deliberate counter-portrait: *"Not equal are the dwellers of the Fire and the dwellers of Paradise. It is the dwellers of Paradise that will be successful"* (59:20). The people of Paradise will ascend to lofty degrees and secure dwellings — *"Abiding therein; excellent it is as an abode and as a place to rest in"* (25:76) — while the people of Hell will go down to the lowest levels and continual regret, with all kinds of punishments and torments, of which Allah says *"Evil indeed it is as an abode and as a place to rest in"* (25:66). And the reason for the difference is stated plainly: the people of Paradise attain what they attain **in return for what they have done of acceptable deeds**, in contrast to the people of Hell, who will not have even one deed to their credit that would qualify them to enter Paradise and be saved from the Fire.

**Why "a place of repose"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the two words. *Mustaqarr* is a permanent residence — where you settle. *Maqīl* is derived from *qaylūlah*, the siesta; so *maqīl* means the place for having a siesta. Maʿārif suggests, citing Qurṭubī, that *maqīl* is probably mentioned here because it is referred to in one of the traditions that on that Day Allah will complete the reckoning of the entire creation by noon, and the people of Paradise will reach Paradise at the time of siesta — as will the condemned reach Hell.

Ibn Kathīr records the same from the early authorities. ʿIkrimah said: "I know the time when the people of Paradise will enter Paradise and the people of Hell will enter Hell. It is the time which in this world is the time when the late forenoon starts and people go back to their families to take a siesta. The people of Hell will go to Hell, but the people of Paradise will be taken to Paradise and will have their siesta in Paradise, and they will be fed the liver of a whale, and they will all eat their fill."

The detail is tender rather than grand. The longest, most terrifying day in existence, and by its noon the believers are already home, resting and fed.

## Living it

**Stop reading your circumstances as a verdict.** Ayah 20 tells you outright that the arrangement of rich and poor, strong and weak, known and unknown is a test — the rich and healthy tested in thankfulness, the poor and sick tried in patience. So the question the ayah leaves hanging — *"will you have patience?"* — is the one that matters about your position.

**Cure envy the way the Prophet ﷺ prescribed.** When you catch yourself measuring upward, turn at once toward those below you in wealth, health, strength and status, and let it become gratitude instead of jealousy — the practice Maʿārif cites from Bukhari, Muslim and Mazharī.

**Watch what your doubts are really made of.** Maʿārif's reading of ayah 21 is that endless clever objections and demands grow in soil where faith in the Hereafter is thin. Strengthen the root and the branches fall away.

**Guard the two conditions.** Ayah 23 does not say their deeds were few — it says they were made scattered dust. Ibn Kathīr's rule is that a deed which is neither sincere nor in accordance with the Laws of Allah is futile. Sincerity and conformity: without both, effort becomes motes in a sunbeam that no hand can close on.

passages.title: The sky splits and the wrongdoer bites his hands
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat lift the curtain on the Day of Resurrection twice over — first on the sky, then on a single human face.
