Ayat 25–26 give the cosmic scene: the heavens torn open, angels descending, and every claim to sovereignty collapsing except one. Ayat 27–29 close in on one man inside that scene, biting his own hands with regret over two things — the path he refused, and the friend he chose. The rendering given in Ibn Kathir opens both scenes with the same words — **"And (remember) the Day…"** — so that the terror outside is set beside a discovery inside: that a friendship cost a man everything.

## Ayah 25 — the sky opened, the angels sent down

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us here of "the terror of the Day of Resurrection and the tremendous events that will happen," among them the splitting of the heavens when they are pierced by the clouds — and he identifies that cloud as the shadow of the magnificent light which dazzles all sight. The angels of heaven will then come down on that Day and surround all creatures at the place of gathering, and then, he says, "the Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, will come to pass judgement." Mujahid connected this ayah to another: *"Do they then wait for anything other than that Allah should come to them in the shadows of the clouds and the angels"* (2:210).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Bayan ul-Qurʼan) fills in the picture. The sky will rip apart and a sort of cloud will descend from it carrying the angels with it — like a canopy coming down from the sky, bearing Allah's refulgence, surrounded by angels. Two points of sequencing follow. First, this will precede the beginning of the reckoning; it is the opening scene of judgement, not its verdict. Second, this ripping is not the same ripping as the one when the *ṣūr* (the Trumpet) is blown to finish off the earth and the sky. Here the sky rips open only to make an opening, and this descent of the cloud takes place *after* the second blowing of the Trumpet, once the earth and the sky have taken their new shape.

The rendering itself strains to hold the scale of it: the angels are not merely sent down, but "sent down, with a grand descending."

## Ayah 26 — "True authority that Day belongs to the Most Compassionate"

Every sovereignty that ever existed in this world was borrowed and provisional. On that Day the ownership is stated plainly and exclusively. Ibn Kathir pairs the ayah with *"Whose is the kingdom this Day? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible!"* (40:16), and then quotes a report he introduces simply as "In the Sahih": that Allah, may He be exalted, will fold up the heavens in His Right Hand and will take the earths in His other Hand, then He will say, *"I am the Sovereign, I am the Judge. Where are the kings of the earth? Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogants?"*

Notice, too, whose sovereignty the ayah names: **ar-Raḥmān**, the Most Compassionate. The commentators here simply let the Name stand; the pause is mine — that the Day of decisive judgement is announced under the Name of mercy.

**"And it will be a hard Day for the disbelievers."** Ibn Kathir explains this to mean "it will be very difficult," and gives the reason: because it will be the Day of justice and the decisive judgement — hard precisely because nothing on it will be crooked. He cites *"Truly, that Day will be a hard Day — far from easy for the disbelievers"* (74:9–10), and then draws the line the ayah itself draws by naming only the disbelievers: as for the believers, *"The greatest terror will not grieve them"* (21:103). The same Day, two utterly different experiences.

## Ayah 27 — the wrongdoer bites his hands

The scene narrows. Ibn Kathir describes the man as one "who rejected the path of the Messenger and what he brought from Allah of clear truth concerning which there is no doubt, and followed another path." When the Day of Resurrection comes the regret finally lands — but, in Ibn Kathir's words, "his regret will avail him nothing, and he will bite on his hands in sorrow and grief."

The ayah says he bites *his two hands*; the translation given renders it "bite his nails," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes him biting his fingers in distress and repentance. The picture is of a man turning his own violence inward because there is no longer anything outward left to do — no argument to make, no companion to appeal to, no time to spend. That last observation is my own reading of the image, not a claim from the commentaries.

Notice, too, what he wishes for. Not simply a path: **"a path with the Messenger."** What he mourns is a road he could have walked in someone's company, and did not.

Ibn Kathir is careful about the identity of this wrongdoer: "Whether this Ayah was revealed concerning ʿUqbah bin Abi Muʿīṭ or someone else among the doomed, **it applies to every wrongdoer**." He compares it to *"On the Day when their faces will be turned over in the Fire"* (33:66). Every wrongdoer, he says, will feel the ultimate regret on the Day of Resurrection, and will bite at his hands saying exactly these words.

## Ayah 28 — the story behind "so-and-so"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the occasion of revelation — noting that the verse was revealed on a particular occasion but that its implication is universal — and it is the key that unlocks the whole passage.

ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayṭ was one of the chieftains of the polytheists in Makkah. Whenever he returned from an expedition he would invite the nobility of the city to dinner, and he used to call on the Prophet ﷺ frequently. On one such occasion he presented food to the Prophet ﷺ, who said he could not eat it until ʿUqbah proclaimed that Allah is One with no one associated with Him in worship, and that he ﷺ is His Messenger. ʿUqbah recited the words, and the Prophet ﷺ ate the dinner according to his promise.

Then his close friend heard about it. ʿUbayy ibn Khalaf was very cross that ʿUqbah had accepted Islam and recited the Kalimah. ʿUqbah tried to defend himself: Muhammad ﷺ was an eminent person of Quraysh, and for him to leave the house without eating would have been degrading for the host — the words were said only to please him. ʿUbayy would not accept the explanation, and told ʿUqbah that if he was really ashamed he should go and spit on the Prophet's ﷺ face. The wretched man obliged his depraved friend and did as suggested.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, on the authority of Baghawi, that Allah disgraced them both in this world as well, both being killed at the battle of Badr — and that this ayah describes the torment awaiting such a man on the Day of Judgement: seeing the torment before him, he bites his fingers in distress and repentance and wishes he had never made ʿUbayy ibn Khalaf his friend in the world. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives this account with the attribution "Mazhari, Qurtubi.")

Sit with the shape of it. ʿUqbah's tongue had already formed the truth. What undid him, on this account, was not an argument, not evidence, not doubt about the message — it was a friend's contempt.

## Why the Qur'an says "so-and-so" and not a name

The ayah does not name ʿUbayy. It says **fulān** — "so-and-so." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Tafsir Mazhari, points precisely at this: although these verses were revealed in respect of ʿUqbah, the moral of the verse is universal, and the use of the word *fulān* is what alludes to that universality.

The classical scholars did differ over the identity behind the blank. Ibn Kathir leaves it open — "whether this refers to Umayyah bin Khalaf or his brother Ubayy bin Khalaf, or to someone else" — and defines the man by his function rather than his name: "the one among the propagators of misguidance who diverted him from true guidance and led him to follow the path of misguidance." The sources Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows name ʿUbayy ibn Khalaf specifically. Either way, by the Qur'an's own choice of *fulān*, the lesson is not confined to one man's history.

## Ayah 29 — "He led me astray from the Reminder"

**"The Reminder"** — *adh-dhikr* — means the Qur'an, says Ibn Kathir; and "after it had come to me" means, in his words, "after it had reached me." This is the sharpest edge of the passage. The man's ruin was not that the truth never arrived. It arrived, and reached him.

Then the ayah closes with a line the wrongdoer does not say — Allah says it: **"And Shaytan is to man ever a deserter."** Ibn Kathir explains the work Shaytan does: "he leads him away from the truth and diverts him from it, and uses him for the purposes of falsehood and calls him to it." The classical rendering adds a clarifying phrase to the word: a deserter *"(in the hour of need)."*

There is something quietly striking in the placement — and here I am reflecting rather than reporting: the man spends ayah 28 blaming his friend, and Allah's own comment is not a denial but a widening, so that behind the human friend stands the one who deserts a person exactly when he is needed.

## From the Sunnah — on choosing company

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical lesson: when two friends get together in acts of immorality and sin and help each other in performing forbidden deeds, the same will apply to them, and they will be remorseful and feel sorry for their friendship in the Hereafter. It then cites three narrations:

- **Musnad Ahmed, Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud** and others, on the authority of Sayyidna Abu Saʿid al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ once said, in the rendering given: "Do not make a non-Muslim your friend and your possessions should be used only by the pious persons." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses the point as: do not have the non-pious as your friend.
- **Bukhari**, reported from Sayyidna Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), rendered: "Every person is influenced by the faith and way of life of his friends." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the consequence — "therefore, one must be very mindful when selecting his friends." The narration's word for the friend, *khalīl*, is the very word ayah 28 uses.
- **al-Bazzar**, reported from Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and given with the attribution "Qurtubi": the Prophet ﷺ was asked what sort of friends we should keep in our company, and answered — "The one who reminds you of Allah when you see him, and adds to your knowledge when he speaks, and reminds you of the Hereafter when he acts."

Read that last narration beside ayah 28 and the contrast is hard to miss. On the account Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives, ʿUbayy was the exact inverse of that description at every point.

## Living it

What follows is application and personal reflection rather than commentary from the sources.

The passage puts one concrete question in front of a reader: **who is your fulān?** Not who is your enemy — the ayah is not about enemies. It is about a *khalīl*, an intimate friend: the person whose disapproval is hardest to bear.

Three things follow.

First, the regrets in ayat 27 and 28 look like one regret seen from two sides. "Would that I had taken a path with the Messenger" and "would that I had never taken so-and-so as an intimate friend" sit in consecutive breaths.

Second, ayah 29 removes the comfort of ignorance. The Reminder had already come — Ibn Kathir's gloss is that it had already reached him. Knowing the truth is not the finish line.

Third, the passage is anchored by a Name — *ar-Raḥmān*, whose sovereignty on that Day is the true one (ayah 26). The Day is described as hard on the disbelievers, and it is the same Day of which Allah says of the believers, *"The greatest terror will not grieve them"* (21:103). The regret described here belongs to a man who has run out of time. Anyone reading these ayat has not.

passages.title: A Quran abandoned, and why it came piece by piece
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** In ayah 30 the Messenger ﷺ turns to his Lord with a complaint that has echoed ever since: *my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned*. Everything that follows answers that complaint. Ayah 31 consoles him — every prophet before him faced the same enemies. Ayat 32–33 answer the specific objection the deniers used to justify turning away: why did this Book not come down in one piece? And ayah 34 shows where the road of that objection ends.

The thread running through all five ayat is the Qur'an itself: a Book abandoned by those who should have embraced it, defended by the One who sent it, and delivered piece by piece precisely so that the heart carrying it would not break.

## Ayah 30: the Messenger's complaint

Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah tells us how His Messenger and Prophet Muhammad ﷺ will say, "O my Lord! Verily, my people deserted this Qur'an."

The idolaters would not listen to it. Ibn Kathir points to Allah's own description of their tactic elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"And those who disbelieve say: 'Listen not to this Qur'an, and make noise in the midst of it'"* (41:26). Ibn Kathir explains what that looked like in practice: when the Prophet ﷺ would recite the Qur'an to them, they would talk nonsense or start speaking about something else, so that they would not hear it.

Picture that. Not an argument, not a rebuttal — just noise, deliberately raised so that the words could not land. That is the first and crudest form of abandoning the Qur'an.

**When was this complaint made?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a genuine difference of opinion among the commentators: is this a complaint the Prophet ﷺ will make on the Day of Judgement, or one he made during his lifetime? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says both views appear valid, but leans toward the second — because the verse that follows reads as a consolation, which suggests the complaint was made in his lifetime and the next ayah came down to settle his heart. Ibn Kathir renders it in the future tense: "the Messenger *will say*." Where the scholars have genuinely differed, it is honest to hold both and see the weight of each.

## What "abandoning the Qur'an" actually means

This is the heart of the passage, and Ibn Kathir does something remarkable here. Rather than confining "abandonment" to the loud dismissal of the Makkan idolaters, he opens the word out into a series of quieter desertions. In his words, the noise-making of the idolaters is one form of forsaking the Qur'an and rejecting it — **and then**:

- **not believing in it** is the same as forsaking it;
- **not pondering its meanings and trying to understand it** is the same as forsaking it;
- **not acting upon it**, following its commandments and heeding its prohibitions, is the same as forsaking it;
- **turning away from it in favour of poetry or other words or songs or idle talk or some other way** is the same as forsaking it.

Read that list slowly. Each step is a smaller distance from the Book than the one before, and Ibn Kathir gives each the same name. A person may never mock a single ayah and still, by his measure, be counted among those who have forsaken it.

Ibn Kathir does not end that passage with a rebuke but with a prayer, and it is worth carrying: he asks Allah, the Most Generous, the Bestower of bounty, the One able to do what He wills, to keep us safe from doing what earns His wrath and to use us for what earns His pleasure — the preserving and understanding of His Book, and following its commandments night and day in the manner He loves and which pleases Him, for He is Generous and Kind.

## A warning meant for us, not only for them

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection: on the face of it, "abandoning" the Qur'an means denying it or refusing to accept it, and that is what you would expect from disbelievers, not from Muslims. But it then reports that in certain narrations, Muslims who *do* believe in the Qur'an and yet neither read it nor try to follow it fall as much within the reach of this same description.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Sayyidnā Anas ؓ as reporting that the Prophet ﷺ said that the person who has learnt the Qur'an and then hung it up — neither reciting it routinely nor pondering over its injunctions — will be brought on the Day of Resurrection with the Qur'an hanging from his neck by a sling, complaining before Allah: *"This servant of Yours had abandoned me, so decide between me and him."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the source of this report as Qurṭubī.

Notice the terrible symmetry with ayah 30. In ayah 30 it is the Messenger ﷺ who complains that the Book was abandoned. In this report it is the Book itself that complains — and the complaint is against a believer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's heading is blunt: **abandoning the following of the Qur'an is a great sin.**

## Ayah 31: you are not the first

*"Thus have We made for every Prophet an enemy among the criminals."*

Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: just as there are for you, O Muhammad ﷺ, those people who scorned the Qur'an, so in all the previous nations did Allah make for every Prophet an enemy among the criminals — people who called others to their misguidance and disbelief. He connects this to Allah's words, *"And so We have appointed for every Prophet enemies — Shayāṭīn among mankind and Jinn"* (6:112).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the pastoral point: if your adversaries do not accept the Qur'an, this is nothing new. In the past too, people defied Our message, and the messengers had to contend with that. The best course for you as well, it says, is to be contented.

There is a specific kind of comfort here. The ayah does not promise that the opposition will stop; it reframes it. Opposition is not evidence that something has gone wrong with the mission — it is what every prophet met. And the word Allah uses for the enemies is *al-mujrimīn*, the criminals: it locates the fault in them, not in the message or the one carrying it.

**"But sufficient is your Lord as a Guide and Helper."** Ibn Kathir explains that for the one who follows His Messenger and believes in His Book, Allah will be his Guide and Helper in this world and the Hereafter. And he explains why these two names in particular: the idolaters used to try to prevent people from following the Qur'an lest anyone be guided by it — they wanted their way to prevail over the way of the Qur'an. So Allah answers their scheme point for point. They block guidance; He is the Guide. They fight to make their way win; He is the Helper. And the ayah's own word — *sufficient* — closes the matter: when Allah is your Guide and your Helper, nothing further is needed.

## Ayah 32: "Why was it not sent down all at once?"

Ibn Kathir frames this as one item in a long catalogue: Allah tells us about the many objections raised by the disbelievers, their stubbornness, and how they spoke of things which were none of their concern. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the sequence of objections and answers, which began at the start of the sūrah, is still continuing here.

What exactly were they asking? Ibn Kathir spells it out: why was this Qur'an, which was revealed to him, not sent down all at one time, as the previous Books were — the Tawrāh, the Injīl, the Zabūr and the other Divine Books? It sounds like a scholarly question. It was not. It was a demand that revelation conform to their expectations, and behind it lay the suggestion that a Book arriving in instalments was somehow less than a Book handed down complete.

Allah's answer does not apologise. It reveals the purpose: *"Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby. And We have revealed it to you gradually, in stages."*

Ibn Kathir explains that it was revealed in stages over twenty-three years, according to events and circumstances and whatever rulings were needed, in order to strengthen the hearts of the believers — and he links this to *"And (it is) a Qur'an which We have divided (into parts)"* (17:106).

On the closing words *wa rattalnāhu tartīlā*, Ibn Kathir preserves two readings from the early authorities: **Qatādah** said it means "We have explained it," and **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam** said it means "We have given its interpretation." So the staged delivery is not merely a schedule — on these two readings it is bound up with the Book being made clear.

## How coming in pieces strengthened the heart

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the mechanism in three concrete ways:

**1. It made memorisation possible.** It was made easy for him to remember the Qur'an by heart; if the whole Book had been revealed in one go, holding it by heart would not have been that easy. And remembrance of the Qur'an by heart, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, expelled all worries from his heart.

**2. It matched the medicine to the wound.** Whenever the disbelievers raised an objection or inflicted some mistreatment, a verse would be revealed to give him fortitude. Had the entire Qur'an been revealed in one piece with the fortitude for that special occasion mentioned somewhere inside it, searching it out would have been painstaking — and it would have been uncertain whether or not his attention would be drawn to the particular verse.

**3. The timing itself was the proof.** An instant response by way of revelation, answering awkward questions, was by itself the confirmation of Allah's support — and that, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is the biggest source of strength for the heart.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a careful qualification: the wisdom of keeping the heart strong is not dependent on gradual revelation alone. Other factors are mentioned elsewhere, as in *"And We have divided the Qur'an into portions, so that you may recite it to the people gradually"* (17:106). (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Bayān ul-Qurʼān here.)

**The two descents.** Ibn Kathir records that Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Nasāʼī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The Qur'an was sent down all at once to the first heaven on Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power), then it was revealed over twenty years." So there is a sense in which the Qur'an *did* descend complete and in one act — to the first heaven, on Laylat al-Qadr. What reached the Prophet ﷺ in instalments was its release into the life of a man and a community.

## Ayah 33: the promise that no argument will stand

*"And no example or similitude do they bring, but We reveal to you the truth, and the better explanation thereof."*

Ibn Kathir explains "no example or similitude do they bring" as meaning no arguments or doubts. And the answer: they do not say anything in an attempt to oppose the truth without Allah responding to them with the truth of that same matter — more clearly and more eloquently than anything they say.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees this ayah as supporting and accentuating the wisdom just described: it promises Allah's support in any situation of awkward questions asked by the deniers. Read the two ayat together and the logic locks: *why is it coming piece by piece?* Because each piece is an answer arriving exactly when it is needed — and here is the guarantee that no challenge will ever arrive without its answer.

Look closely at what is promised. Not merely a rebuttal, but *aḥsana tafsīran* — "the better explanation." The reply Allah supplies does not just neutralise the objection; it comes more clearly and more eloquently than anything the objectors said. This is the confidence a believer can carry into any conversation about this Book.

## Ayah 34: where that road ends

*"Those who will be gathered to Hell on their faces, such will be in an evil state, and most astray from the path."*

Ibn Kathir marks the turn: Allah now tells us about the terrible state of the disbelievers when they are raised on the Day of Resurrection and gathered into Hell. His heading over this whole section names the three movements together — the reason the Qur'an was revealed in stages, the refutation of the disbelievers, and their evil end.

Ibn Kathir reports that in the Ṣaḥīḥ, it is reported from Anas that a man said, "O Messenger of Allah, how will the disbeliever be gathered on his face on the Day of Resurrection?" The Prophet ﷺ said: **"The One Who caused him to walk on his two feet is able to make him walk on his face on the Day of Resurrection."**

That answer is worth sitting with. The question assumes a difficulty; the reply removes it by pointing to the One whose power gave the man his walk in the first place. We affirm that power exactly as the ayah and the ḥadīth state it, without likening it to anything in creation and without explaining it away.

## Living it

The passage puts one question in front of a believer, and Ibn Kathir has already framed it: on his reckoning, abandonment is not a single act but a slope, and the last step on it — turning away from the Qur'an in favour of idle talk or amusement — is one almost anyone can take without noticing.

So the practical shape of these ayat is small and daily. **Recite it**, so that it is not a book learnt and then hung up. **Ponder it**, since Ibn Kathir counts failure to seek its meaning as a form of forsaking it in its own right. **Act on it** — its commandments and its prohibitions — because he counts that too. And when the Book asks something hard of you, remember why it came the way it did: piece by piece, timed to the moment, sent by a Lord who is *sufficient* as a Guide and a Helper.

passages.title: Destroyed nations from Moses to the ruined city
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** Allah turns the eyes of the Makkan idolaters backwards — to Musa and Harun, to Nuh, to 'Ad and Thamud and the Dwellers of ar-Rass, and finally to a ruined town the Quraysh themselves had passed by. Six ayat, one argument: rejecting a messenger is not a new invention, and it has never once ended well.

Ibn Kathir heads this section **"Frightening the Idolators of Quraysh."** Allah, he says, threatens the idolaters who denied and opposed His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, and warns them of the punishment and painful torment He sent upon the previous nations who rejected their Messengers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the same way: the point being pressed is that rebuffing prophets and the message they brought has been the common practice of people through the ages, and a few well-known cases are named to give that assertion weight. By drawing a parallel with the past generations, Maʿārif says, it is made plain that the pagans of Makkah would not listen to any reason — in this respect they were no better than the animals, or even worse.

Notice the shape of the passage. It begins with a Prophet who was *given* something — the Book, and a brother; it moves through nations that were *shown* the proof; and it ends with a ruin that is simply *there*, beside the road. The passage narrows from sacred history down to a place the audience could see with their own eyes.

## Musa and Harun — Allah does not send a messenger unsupported (ayah 35)

"And indeed We gave Musa the Scripture, and placed his brother Harun with him as a helper."

Ibn Kathir explains the second half: Harun was placed with Musa **as a helper** — that is, as another Prophet who helped and supported him. This is worth pausing on. The mission to Fir'awn and his chiefs was not laid on one man alone; Allah answered the weight of the task with the companionship of a brother. For a Prophet ﷺ who was himself being denied and opposed by his own people, and for anyone carrying truth into a hostile room, that is not a small detail.

## "The people who have denied Our signs" (ayah 36)

Musa and Harun are told: *"Go you both to the people who have denied Our Ayat."* Ibn Kathir records what followed: Fir'awn and his chiefs denied them both.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a fine question here, quoting Bayān ul-Qur'ān. What "signs" had they denied? The Tawrāh had not yet been revealed to Musa (عليه السلام) at that time, so it cannot be the Tawrāh that was denied. The answer offered is that what they had denied was either **the proofs of the Oneness of Allah** — which anyone can understand according to his own mental level — or **the traditions of the past prophets**, passed on through the generations, no matter in how little detail. The Qur'an speaks that way elsewhere, as in *"Yusuf brought you the clear signs before"* (40:34), where a people are held answerable for the teachings of an earlier prophet that had reached them.

This closes a door people like to leave open. A person who has never held a scripture is not therefore blank. The evidence of one Creator, and whatever survives of prophetic teaching in a culture's memory, is already a summons — and can already be refused.

Then: *"Then We destroyed them with utter destruction."* Ibn Kathir sets alongside it: *"Allah destroyed them completely, and similar (awaits) the disbelievers"* (47:10). The "similar" is the sting. The Makkans are not being handed history; they are being handed a forecast.

## Nuh — denying one messenger is denying them all (ayah 37)

"And Nuh's people, when they denied **the Messengers**, We drowned them." Allah sent only Nuh to them. So why the plural?

Ibn Kathir gives the principle: *whoever denies one Messenger denies all the Messengers, because there is no difference between one Messenger and another.* If it had so happened that Allah had sent all His Messengers to them, they would have denied them all. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same from the other side: those people had neither seen the past prophets nor rejected them, but in denying Nuh (عليه السلام) they had by implication rejected all the prophets, because the principles of religion expounded by all the prophets are essentially the same — so rejecting one is tantamount to rejecting all.

This is a foundation of belief, not a rhetorical flourish. Prophethood is a single message carried by many mouths. To pick and choose among the messengers is to have understood none of them.

Ibn Kathir then fills in what the ayah compresses: Nuh stayed among his people **950 years**, calling them to Allah and warning them of His punishment — *"And none believed with him, except a few"* (11:40). Nine and a half centuries of patient calling; a handful of believers. For this reason Allah drowned them all and — in Ibn Kathir's striking phrase — left no one among the sons of Adam alive on earth apart from those who boarded the boat.

**"And We made them a sign for mankind."** A sign, says Ibn Kathir, means *a lesson to be learned*. He connects it to *"Verily, when the water rose beyond its limits, We carried you in the boat. That We might make it a remembrance for you, and the keen ear may understand it"* (69:11–12), which he glosses: Allah left for you ships that you ride upon to travel across the depths of the seas, so that you may remember the blessing of Allah towards you when He saved you from drowning, and made you the descendants of those who believed in Allah and followed His commandments.

So every vessel afloat is a quiet reminder of the Flood, and you are counted among the descendants of the people who got on board. That is what "a sign for mankind" means: not a museum piece, but an inheritance you are living inside.

The ayah closes: *"And We have prepared a painful torment for the wrongdoers."* The drowning was this world's instalment. The account is not settled at the water's edge.

## 'Ad, Thamud, the Dwellers of ar-Rass — and generations beyond counting (ayah 38)

Ibn Kathir passes over 'Ad and Thamud quickly: their story is referred to in more than one sūrah, such as Sūrat al-A'rāf, and there is no need to repeat it here. The interesting case is **the Dwellers of ar-Rass**.

Two early reports are preserved. Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ibn 'Abbās that the Dwellers of ar-Rass were **the people of one of the villages of Thamud**. Ath-Thawrī narrated from Abu Bukayr from 'Ikrimah that **ar-Rass was a well where they buried (*rassū*) their Prophet** — the name of the place preserving the crime committed at it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Bayān ul-Qur'ān) is candid about how little is firmly known. In Arabic, *rass* means **an unlined well** — a pit sunk into the ground without masonry. Neither the Qur'an nor any authentic tradition describes these people in any detail; whatever information is available about them comes through Israelite traditions, which differ from one another. It is more likely, it says, that the remaining people of Thamud had settled down near a well; and how they were tormented is not mentioned in the Qur'an or in any tradition at all.

That restraint is itself a lesson in method. Where the sources are silent, the scholars stayed silent. A believer loses nothing by saying "we do not know" about the details, because the Qur'an did not mention these people to satisfy curiosity — it mentioned them as a warning.

**"And many generations in between."** The word is *qurūn* — nations, says Ibn Kathir, many more than have been mentioned here, all of them destroyed. He compares *"And how many generations have We destroyed after Nuh!"* (17:17) and *"Then, after them, We created other generations"* (23:42).

What is a *qarn*? Ibn Kathir reports the attempts to fix it as a span of years — some defined it as 120 years, others as one hundred, or eighty, or forty. **The most correct view**, he holds, is that a generation is not a number at all but a **cohort**: nations who are one another's contemporaries, living at the same time; when they go and others succeed them, that is another generation. He cites, as recorded in **the Two Sahihs**: *"The best of generations is my generation, then the one that follows it, then the one that follows that."*

That definition changes how you hear the ayah. "Many generations in between" is not a measure of centuries; it is crowd after crowd of human beings who lived, denied, and were swept away.

## No nation was destroyed without warning (ayah 39)

*"And for each We put forward examples, and each We brought to utter ruin."*

The first half is the mercy inside the terror. Ibn Kathir explains it as: *We showed them the proof and gave them clear evidence.* And he quotes Qatādah's four-word summary — **"They had no excuse."** Not one of these nations was struck out of the blue. Every one had the argument put to it plainly, and every one had its chance to answer.

The second half Ibn Kathir glosses simply: *We destroyed them completely.* Two halves, one law: clear proof first, then total ruin. Never the second without the first.

## The ruined city on the road (ayah 40)

Now the argument comes home. *"And indeed they have passed by the town on which was rained the evil rain."*

Ibn Kathir identifies it as the town of the people of Lut, which was called Sodom, and describes the way Allah dealt with it: **He destroyed it by turning it upside down and by sending upon it the rain of stones of baked clay**. He gathers the other places the Qur'an presses this: *"And We rained on them a rain. And how evil was the rain of those who had been warned!"* (27:58); *"Verily, you pass by them in the morning. And at night; will you not then reflect?"* (37:137–138); *"And verily, they were right on the highroad"* (15:76); *"They are both on an open highway, plain to see"* (15:79).

Sit with the force of that. This was not a legend from the far side of the world. The ruin lay on a road they actually travelled — they passed by it in the morning and at night, and it stood plain to see. The Qur'an is not asking them to believe a report. It is asking them to look.

*"Did they not then see it?"* — that is, says Ibn Kathir, so that they might learn a lesson from what happened to its inhabitants: punishment for denying the Messenger and going against the commands of Allah.

## Why they saw nothing — the last line of ayah 40

And then the passage delivers its diagnosis: *"Nay! But they used not to expect any resurrection."*

Ibn Kathir: the disbelievers who passed by it did not learn any lesson **because they did not expect any resurrection**, that is, on the Day of Judgement. That is the root of the whole matter: the passage ends not by naming a sin of behaviour but a missing belief.

They had the evidence. They had the ruins, the road, the daily view. What they lacked was the one belief that turns evidence into a lesson: that we will be raised and will answer for ourselves. Strip that out, and a destroyed city is merely bad weather from long ago — a curiosity to remark on and pass by. Keep it in, and the same stones become a sermon.

## Living it

**Read the ruins.** These ayat rebuke sightseeing without reflection. To see a fallen civilisation, or a fallen man, or an old story of arrogance, and feel nothing, is precisely the failure being named here.

**Take the doctrine seriously.** Honouring one prophet while dismissing another is not devotion; on the principle Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif both state, it amounts to denying them all, because the message is one.

**Trust that proof precedes punishment.** Qatādah's "They had no excuse" should settle an anxious heart. Allah does not destroy a people He has not shown the proof and given clear evidence. The justice in these ayat is not arbitrary; it is documented.

**And check the root.** If reminders keep bouncing off, the problem is usually not the reminders. As the ayah says of them, the sight was there — the expectation of standing before Allah was not. Repair that, and everything you look at begins to speak.

passages.title: Mockery, desire as a god, deaf as cattle
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat take us out onto the streets of Makkah, where the Prophet ﷺ is being laughed at, and then they lift the curtain to show what is really going on inside those who laugh. The unit moves in one continuous line: they mock him (41), they let slip that he almost turned them away from their idols (42), Allah names what such a man is really worshipping — his own desire (43), and finally weighs their hearing and understanding against that of grazing cattle and finds them lower (44). The passage is about the difference between having ears and actually hearing.

## The taunt in the street

Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah is telling us how the disbelievers mocked the Messenger ﷺ when they saw him. He connects it to a nearly identical verse in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ — *"And when the disbelievers see you, they take you not except for mockery"* (21:36) — and explains what that mockery consisted of: **they tried to find faults and shortcomings in him.** It was not casual humour. It was the work of men looking for something, anything, to hold up and discredit.

Notice the word *only* in the verse: *"When they see you, they only make fun of you."* Mockery was not one of their responses among others; the verse presents it as the whole of what they did with him. Every sighting produced the same reflex.

Then comes their line: **"Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a Messenger?"** Ibn Kathir says they said this *"by way of belittling and trying to undermine him."* The force of the sneer sits in that one word *this*. Their objection was not offered as an argument. It was an attempt to make the messenger look small.

**And Allah put them in their place.** That is Ibn Kathir's phrase, and it is worth pausing on how Allah does it. He does not answer by listing His Prophet's virtues. He simply widens the frame: *"And indeed Messengers before you were mocked at"* (6:10). The mockery is not evidence that something has gone wrong with this mission. It is the standard reception. If you feel the sting of being laughed at for your faith, this verse tells you that you are standing in a very long line, and at the front of it stand the Messengers of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this the connective tissue of the passage. Commenting on the run of ayat that leads into these — the ones that named earlier peoples who were destroyed — it explains that *"it had been the common practice of the people through the ages to rebuff the prophets and the message they had brought,"* and that a few well-known prophets are mentioned precisely so the pattern is undeniable: they were rejected by their people, and then *"they were subjected to Allah's wrath and were annihilated completely."* That is the backdrop against which our four ayat are heard; the mockery in 25:41 is not a new thing under the sun.

Maʿārif adds a striking observation from that same background: the Qur'ān says the people of Sayyidnā Nūḥ (peace be upon him) rejected *the prophets*, plural, although *"they had neither seen the past prophets nor had they rejected them."* The reason is that *"the principals of religion expounded by all prophets are essentially the same. Hence rejection of one prophet is tantamount to rejection of all."* Reject the message at its root and you have not rejected one man — you have rejected every man who ever carried it.

## The confession hidden inside the insult

Ayah 42 is where their own tongues betray them: *"He would have almost turned us away from our gods, had we not been patient in clinging to them."*

Ibn Kathir spells out what they meant: *"he nearly turned us away from worshipping idols, and he would have done so, had we not been patient and persevered in our ways."* Sit with what they have just admitted. **In the middle of an insult, they concede that he nearly took them.** By their own account, only their digging in kept them where they were — and they said it as a boast.

Their confidence gets one short answer. Ibn Kathir says Allah spoke here *warning and threatening them*: **"And they will know, when they see the torment, who it is that is most astray from the path."** They had set themselves up as judges of who was misguided. Allah does not argue the point now. He lets the verdict wait for the day when the torment is in front of their eyes. *"They will know"* — some things are only learned by being seen.

## When your desire becomes your god

Ayah 43 is the heart of the passage, and it is where the diagnosis turns from behaviour to worship: *"Have you seen him who has taken as his god his own vain desire?"*

Ibn Kathir's gloss is precise and unsparing: it means **"whatever he admires and sees as good in his own desires becomes his religion and his way."** That is a definition worth memorising. The man in this verse has not stopped having a religion. He has one — it is simply that its scripture is his own preference. Whatever appeals to him is his way; the taste of the moment is the final authority.

**Ibn Kathir's parallel.** He reads this alongside *"Is he then, to whom the evil of his deeds is made fair seeming, so that he considers it as good? Verily, Allah sends astray whom He wills"* (35:8). The desire-worshipper does not experience himself as a rebel. His wrongdoing has been made to look good in his own eyes — he looks at it and sees something fine. That is what makes the condition so hard to escape: the faculty that should raise the alarm has itself been recruited.

**Ibn ʿAbbās on the shifting idol.** Ibn Kathir then reports from Ibn ʿAbbās: *"During the Jāhiliyyah, a man would worship a white rock for a while, then if he saw another that looked better, he would worship that and leave the first."* Read that next to the verse and the point lands. The rock was replaceable; what stayed constant was that he followed whatever looked better to him. That is idolatry with the object interchangeable and the preference left standing, which is exactly what ayah 43 names.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān on what this looks like in a believer's life.** Under the heading *"Following forbidden things — a type of idolatry,"* Maʿārif applies the verse without softening it: *"The one who practises forbidden things which are against the tenets of Islam to satisfy his personal desires is described in this verse as the worshiper of his own lust."* And it cites, via Qurṭubī, that Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) *said that the selfish desires are like an idol which is worshipped, and then he recited this verse to prove his point.*

So the verse is not confined to the mockers of Makkah. Wherever a person sets aside what Allah has forbidden in order to satisfy a craving, Maʿārif says this ayah is describing him.

**"Would you then be a guardian over him?"** The verse ends by turning to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir introduces this whole section by saying that Allah is telling His Prophet ﷺ **that if Allah decrees that someone will be misguided and wretched, then no one can guide him except Allah, glory be to Him.** The question put to the Prophet ﷺ is a rhetorical one, and there is mercy in it: he is not the one made responsible for the outcome. And the verse Ibn Kathir quotes says it plainly: *"Verily, Allah sends astray whom He wills"* (35:8). That lifts a weight off the shoulders of everyone who has ever exhausted themselves trying to save someone who does not want saving. Convey, care, pray. The outcome was never your department.

## Ears that do not hear

Ayah 44 delivers the verdict: *"Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like cattle — nay, they are even farther astray from the path."*

Two faculties are named, and the question implies both are missing: hearing and understanding. These men were not short of sound reaching their ears. What was missing was the step after hearing. Note too that the verse says *most of them* — it does not flatten every individual into one judgement.

Then the comparison, and Ibn Kathir refuses to let it be softened: **"they are worse than grazing cattle."** His reasoning is the sharpest sentence in this section of the tafsir:

> *Cattle only do what they were created to do, but these people were created to worship Allah Alone without associating partners with Him, but they worship others with Him, even though evidence has been established against them and Messengers have been sent to them.*

That is the argument in full. An animal is not deficient — it does exactly what it was created to do. The human being was created for the worship of Allah alone, without partners. And these men missed it with every advantage: evidence established against them, and Messengers sent to them. That is why the verse says not merely "like cattle" but **"farther astray."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reaches the same conclusion from its side, summarising the drift of the whole passage: by drawing the parallel with the past generations, it is made clear that *"the pagans of Makkah would not listen to any reason as they were no better than the animals or even worse than that."*

## What this passage asks of us

**Expect the mockery, and read it correctly.** Ayah 41, with 6:10 behind it, resets the meaning of being laughed at for your faith. It is not a sign that the message has failed. Messengers before him were mocked too.

**Notice what stubbornness can look like from the inside.** In ayah 42, by Ibn Kathir's reading, the disbelievers credit their own perseverance for keeping them where they were — while admitting the truth had nearly moved them. Holding a position firmly is not by itself proof that the position is right.

**Audit what actually decides things.** Ibn Kathir's line — *whatever he admires and sees as good in his own desires becomes his religion and his way* — is a test you can apply this week. When Allah's ruling and your preference pull opposite ways, which one moves? And per Maʿārif and Ibn ʿAbbās, doing the forbidden to satisfy a personal desire is the very thing this ayah is describing.

**Distrust the beautification.** Because of 35:8, expect that a wrong you are comfortable with will not feel wrong from the inside. That is why we need revelation and the counsel of others.

**Carry the message, not the outcome.** You are not a guardian over anyone. As Ibn Kathir says, if Allah decrees that someone will be misguided, no one can guide him except Allah, glory be to Him.

**And do not stop at hearing.** Ayah 44 puts hearing and understanding side by side, and Ibn Kathir's reason for the comparison with cattle is that these people had the evidence and the Messengers — and still worshipped others alongside Allah.

passages.title: Signs in shade, night and rain, then the great striving
passages.tafsir:
Ibn Kathir marks the turn: "Here Allah begins explaining the evidence for His existence and His perfect power to create various things and pairs of opposites." What follows is a series of the most ordinary things in the world — the shadow that stretches out before sunrise, the night that falls, sleep, the morning, the wind, the rain — each a pairing of opposites only Allah could hold in balance (shade and sun, night and day, dead earth and living earth, rain sent here and withheld there). Then in ayat 51–52 comes the conclusion: since this is your Lord, do not yield to those who deny Him; carry His Book to people with everything you have.

## The hidden argument: causes are not the Cause

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens with the point that unlocks the whole passage. Allah has tied every created thing to specific causes: crops and grass depend on land, water and air; light on the sun and the moon; rain on clouds and air. And He has bound those causes to their effects so tightly that, as Maʿārif puts it, the solar system has run for centuries without "a split of a second's difference" — no overhaul, no repair, its positions calculable with precision centuries in advance.

Then comes the irony: that very reliability is what made people forgetful. Seeing every effect in the universe linked to a visible cause, they confined their eyes to those causes and began believing them to be the original creator of all these events — "the real power of the Creator which was the original cause of all causes remained hidden behind the covers of visible causes only." Prophets are sent, and divine books revealed, precisely so that human beings rise above this shortsightedness and see behind the cover of apparent causes to the omnipotence of the Creator who is in fact running the whole system.

It is common experience: the sun rises in the east and the shadows are long; they shorten through the morning and are shortest at noon; then they lengthen again until they are longest before sunset. All humanity draws unlimited benefit from this, and everyone can see that these are the effects of the sun's movement between east and west — "but little attention is paid to the question as to who has created this sun and who has bound it to a well-planned system." And the answer to that question, Maʿārif says, "cannot be found by one's eyes, but it can be perceived by the insight of heart and mind."

## Ayat 45–46: the shade, and how it is taken back

**What the shade refers to.** Ibn Kathir reports from a remarkable list of early authorities — Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Abū Mālik, Masrūq, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, an-Nakhaʿī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, as-Suddī "and others" — that the shade here refers to "the period from the beginning of the dawn until the sun rises": the cool, shadowed hour before sunrise, when the whole earth lies in shade.

**"He could have made it still."** *Sākinan* means, in Ibn Kathir's words, "immobile, never changing" — and he links it to the challenge elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"Say: Tell me! If Allah made the night continuous for you…"* (28:71). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks you to sit with what a frozen world would mean: wherever there was sunlight it would have stayed sunlight forever, and wherever there was shade it would have remained shade forever. Neither humans nor any other living creatures could survive perpetual sun; and, Maʿārif adds, perpetual shade is no kinder — they could not survive that either. In His wisdom Allah did not freeze them, but made them move.

**The sun as evidence.** "But We have made the sun its guide" — *dalīlan*, a guide or indicator. Ibn Kathir explains: "were it not for the sun rising, it would not be there, for a thing can only be known in contrast to its opposite." Qatādah and as-Suddī add: "The sun is a guide which follows the shade until the shade disappears."

**"Then We withdraw it towards Ourselves — a gradual withdrawal"** (ayah 46). Ibn Kathir notes that "it" is the shade; *yasīran* means slowly. As-Suddī describes "a gentle, concealed, withdrawal until there is no shade left on earth except under a roof or a tree, and the sun is shining on whatever is above it." Ayyūb bin Mūsā said simply: "Little by little." It is never still, and it is never seen moving. That is the force of *qabḍan yasīran*: Allah's management of the world is continuous and imperceptible at once.

**On "towards Ourselves."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here. Allah, it says, "is beyond the purview of body or direction and hence there is no question of the shade being pulled toward Him." The phrase conveys, rather, that "shortening of the shades takes place by His Supreme Power."

## Ayah 47: night as clothing, sleep as a cutting-off, day as a rising

**Night is *libās*, clothing.** Ibn Kathir: "It covers and conceals all things," citing *"By the night as it envelops"* (92:1). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that night covers up everything "like a natural sheet as does the dress to human body." Night does that for the earth every day, and we have stopped noticing.

**Sleep is *subāt*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the word to the root *sabt*, which means "to cut out" — *subāt* is "that thing which cuts out some other thing." Sleep is what cuts away the exhaustion and fatigue built up by a day's work: "In sleep one is cut off with stress and strain of mind and body while they are rested," which is why the word is usually rendered rest, relaxation or tranquillity. Ibn Kathir explains it as "a halt to movement so that bodies may rest," because the faculties and limbs get tired from their constant movement during the day when one goes out to earn a living; when night comes and it becomes quiet, they stop moving and rest, "so sleep provides a rejuvenation for both the body and the soul."

**Day is *nushūr*, a rising and dispersal.** Ibn Kathir: "people get up and go out to earn a living and attend to their business," citing *"It is out of His mercy that He has made for you the night and the day that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty"* (28:73). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes why *revival* is the right image: the opposite of the day, that is sleep, "is like death when one loses all his senses" — so morning is a revival.

**The argument from sleep that most people never make.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds three blessings stacked inside this one ayah. First, that night is dark and cool — matched to a nature that finds it very difficult to sleep in daylight and wakes quickly if it does. Second, that sleep itself restores. Third, the subtle one: that the entire humanity and the animals sleep at night instinctively. Imagine if sleeping times differed from person to person — some asleep while others moved about for their work, the noise disturbing the sleepers, and, worse, people unable to help one another, "because working time of one would have been the time of rest for the other." Could humanity have solved this by a social contract instead? Maʿārif answers that it would not have been easy in the first place to make billions of people agree on a single resolution; enforcing such a contract would have required many formal departments, and there would still have been room for violation through corrupt means. Instead Allah instilled the schedule in our nature: the urge to sleep at night is such that "one can keep awake only with great difficulty and effort." He fixed common timings for other needs too — all people feel hungry in the mornings and evenings, so our eating times are shared.

## Ayat 48–50: the winds, the rain, and who receives it

**The winds go ahead as good news.** Ibn Kathir observes that the winds are of many different types, depending on the purpose for which they are sent: some form the clouds, others carry or drive them, others come ahead of the clouds as heralds announcing their coming, some come earlier still to stir up the earth, and some "fertilize" or "seed" the clouds to make it rain. And the winds arrive *before* the mercy — the gust that makes you look up is itself the glad tidings.

**"Pure water."** *Ṭahūr*, Ibn Kathir says, means water sent down "as a means of purifying." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens it: in Arabic *ṭahūr* means something pure in itself which also purifies other things — Allah gave water both properties at once. Maʿārif follows the water's whole journey: down from the clouds as rain, hail or snow; some flowing over the surface, the rest seeping into a natural underground drainage system that carries it to every corner of the earth and returns it at the surface as springs and fountains, or is reached by digging wells. All of it — rainwater, rivers, streams and canals, water preserved underground — is pure in the Sharīʿah and retains the inherent property of cleaning other things; on this, Maʿārif states, there is consensus of opinion in the ummah, and it is the express purport of the Qur'an and Sunnah.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites what Abū Saʿīd said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked whether wuḍūʼ could be performed with the water of the well of Buḍāʿah, a well into which rubbish and the flesh of dogs were thrown. He ﷺ replied, *"Water is pure and nothing makes it impure."* Ibn Kathir notes that it was recorded by ash-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad, who graded it Ṣaḥīḥ, and also by Abū Dāwūd and at-Tirmidhī, who graded it Ḥasan, and by an-Nasāʼī.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the fiqh that grows from the ayah: a large body of water — a pond, pool or canal — remains pure even if something filthy falls into it, on which there is also general consensus, unless the effect of the filth is perceptible and the water's colour, taste or smell changes. Where the quantity of water is small, the jurists (*mujtahidūn*) differed over the nature and quantity of the filth and the quantity of the water; Maʿārif refers the reader to Mazharī, Qurṭubī and the books of fiqh rather than settling it.

**The dead land** (ayah 49). Ibn Kathir describes a land "that waited a long time for rain," devoid of vegetation or anything at all — and then the rain comes and "it becomes alive and its hills are covered with all kinds of colorful flowers," as in *"but when We send down water to it, it is stirred to life and growth"* (41:39). Then the water reaches throats: animals such as cattle drink from it, and "people who are in desperate need of water can drink from it and water their crops and fruits" — recalling *"And He it is Who sends down the rain after they have despaired"* (42:28) and *"Look then at the effects of Allah's mercy, how He revives the earth after its death"* (30:50).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on one word: *anāsiyya*, the plural of *insiyy* — some linguists take it as a plural of *insān* — in the phrase "many cattle and humans." Why *many* rather than all? Because, Maʿārif answers, the reference is to the cattle and human beings of the jungles and deserts, who use rainwater directly; city dwellers normally use the water of wells and canals.

**Rain is apportioned, and the apportioning is a message** (ayah 50). Ibn Kathir paraphrases *ṣarrafnāhu*: "We cause rain to fall on this land and not on that, and We cause the clouds to pass over one land and go to another, where We cause sufficient rain to fall so that its people have plenty, but not one drop falls on the first land." There is, he says, a reason and great wisdom behind this. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "One year does not have more rain than another, but Allah distributes the rain as He wills" — and then this very ayah was recited. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿAbbās and explains it: the aggregate amount of water sent down to the world each year is equal; what changes, by Allah's will, is its allocation between territories. Sometimes the quantity is curtailed for a particular habitation as a punishment and a warning; sometimes it is increased for a particular population, again as a punishment for their misdeeds — so water that was a blessing in its origin turns into a torment for people who are ungrateful and disobedient.

*Li-yadhdhakkarū* — "so that they may remember." Remember what? Ibn Kathir gives two answers: that the One who brings the dead earth back to life is able to bring the dead and dry bones back to life; and that those from whom rain is withheld may recognise they are suffering this because of some sin they have committed, so that they may give it up.

**"But most people refuse all but ingratitude."** ʿIkrimah said this refers to those who say that rain comes because of such and such a star. Ibn Kathir notes that ʿIkrimah's view is similar to the authentic ḥadīth recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: one day after a night's rain, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to his Companions, "Do you know what your Lord says?" They said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He ﷺ said that Allah says: *"This morning some of My servants became believers in Me, and some became disbelievers. As for the one who said, 'We have been given rain by the mercy and grace of Allah,' he is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the stars. As for the one who said, 'We have been given rain by such and such a star,' he is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the stars."*

That ḥadīth is the whole passage in miniature. Two people stand in the same rain. One sees a cause and stops there; the other sees through the cause to the Lord who sent it. The rain did not distinguish them — their words did.

## Ayat 51–52: the conclusion drawn from all of it

"Had We willed, We could have raised a warner in every town." Ibn Kathir reads this as: calling them to Allah — but instead "We have singled you out, O Muhammad, to be sent to all the people of earth, and We have commanded you to convey the Qur'an." Note what the ayah does *not* say: not that a warner in every town was beyond Allah's power, but that He willed otherwise and gave one Messenger the whole earth. Ibn Kathir gathers the ayat that make the same claim: *"that I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach"* (6:19); *"but those of the sects that reject it, the Fire will be their promised meeting place"* (11:17); *"that you may warn the Mother of the Towns and all around it"* (42:7); *"Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah"* (7:158). And from the Two Ṣaḥīḥs he cites the Prophet's ﷺ words, *"I have been sent to the red and the black,"* and *"A Prophet would be sent to his own people, but I have been sent to all of mankind."*

**"So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it, a great striving."** Everything turns on one small pronoun, *bihi* — "with **it**." Ibn Kathir says it means with the Qur'an, and notes that this was the view of Ibn ʿAbbās. The weapon named in ayah 52 is the recited Book.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point plainly: this is a Makkan verse, from a time when the injunction for jihād in the sense of fighting the disbelievers had not yet been revealed. What is ordained here "is that you spread the message of Qur'an among the people at large" — and the ayah calls that *jihādan kabīran*, a **great** striving. Maʿārif's conclusion: propagation of the Qur'anic message among people and making them understand it is great Jihad, "whether it is by mouth, pen or any other means." Ibn Kathir sets *jihādan kabīran* alongside *"O Prophet! Strive hard against the disbelievers and the hypocrites"* (9:73).

**Do not obey** those who reject the message. And **strive with the Qur'an** — the answer to rejection is not withdrawal and not compromise, but more Qur'an: recited, explained, carried to whoever will listen.

## Living it

The passage trains a habit of sight. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's answer to "who created this sun and bound it to a well-planned system?" is that the eyes cannot find it — it is perceived by the insight of heart and mind. So the first thing these ayat ask is that you stop letting the visible mechanism satisfy you. You know why it rains; ayah 50 asks who apportioned it, and why here and not there.

The second is gratitude for what is too regular to notice — a shadow that shortens without ever seeming to move, a night that covers the world like a garment, sleep that cuts the day's exhaustion away and hands your body back in the morning. The passage's own verdict in ayah 50 is *fa-abā aktharu'n-nāsi illā kufūran*: most refuse everything but ingratitude. The ḥadīth in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim shows how narrow the gap between the two camps can be — one sentence spoken about the weather.

The third is ayah 52: if the Qur'an is the instrument of the great striving, a believer's share in that striving is measured by how much of it he carries and passes on — by mouth, by pen, or by any other means.

passages.title: The Creator of seas and kinship, and the warner who asks no wage
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat move from the world outside you to the One who made it, and then to the man sent to tell you about Him. Allah points to two things everybody has touched — water and family — shows that both are His arrangement, and then contrasts that living, giving power with the dead idols people prefer; the passage closes by telling the Prophet ﷺ what his job actually is (ayah 56), what he charges for it (ayah 57), and where he is to rest his weight while he does it (ayah 58).

The joint that holds the sequence together is a single quiet argument: **the One who provides is the One who deserves worship, and the messenger who points you to Him wants nothing from you.**

*Backdrop.* Ibn Kathir carries the two preceding ayat into his comment on our passage, so it is worth a sentence. Allah says, "And had We willed, We would have raised a warner in every town" (ayah 51) — and Ibn Kathir reads this as: Allah could have called each locality to Himself through its own warner, but instead He singled out Muhammad ﷺ to be sent to all the people of the earth, and commanded him to convey the Qur'an. He gathers the verses that say the same: "that I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach" (6:19); "that you may warn the Mother of the Towns and all around it" (42:7); "Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah" (7:158). And in the Two Sahihs it is reported that the Prophet ﷺ said, **"I have been sent to the red and the black,"** and, "...A Prophet would be sent to his own people, but I have been sent to all of mankind." Ayah 52 then says, "So obey not the disbelievers, but strive hard against them **with it**" — with what? Ibn Kathir: "meaning, with the Qur'an. This was the view of Ibn 'Abbas." That is the setting into which ayah 53 arrives.

## Ayah 53: the two waters

**"And it is He Who has let free the two seas, this is palatable and sweet, and that is salty and bitter; and He has set a barrier and a complete partition between them."**

Feel the Arabic. *Maraja* (مَرَجَ), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, means to let off or to allow to roam freely — which is why a pasture, the open ground where animals graze and roam about, is called *maraj*. Allah did not merely place the two waters side by side; He let them loose. And yet they never trespass.

Each water is named with a pair of words:

- **ʿadhb** (عَذْب) — sweet water; **furāt** (فُرَات) — delicious and pleasant. Not merely drinkable: enjoyable.
- **milḥ** (مِلْح) — salty; **ujāj** (أُجَاج) — bitter. Ibn Kathir adds: salty, bitter, and *not easy to swallow*.

**Which two seas?** Ibn Kathir is careful here, and his carefulness is instructive. He reports the view of Ibn Jurayj and of Ibn Jarīr that the sweet water is the water of rivers, springs and wells — and says this is the meaning without a doubt, "for nowhere in creation is there a sea which is fresh and sweet." The ayah is not describing an exotic curiosity; it is describing the ordinary, verifiable world. Allah has told us about reality, Ibn Kathir says, "so that His servants may realize His blessings to them and give thanks to Him." The sweet water is the water that flows *amidst people* — Allah has portioned it out among His creatures according to their needs, rivers and springs in every land, according to what they need for themselves and their lands.

The salty water is the seas known in east and west — Ibn Kathir names them: the Atlantic Ocean and the Straits that lead to it, the Red Sea, the Arabian Sea, the Persian Gulf, the China Sea, the Indian Ocean, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea. They do not flow away as rivers do; they are stable, swelling and surging in winter and when the winds are strong, with tides that ebb and flood on a monthly rhythm. "Allah, may He be glorified, the One Whose power is absolute, has set these laws in motion."

**Why salt?** Here both commentaries converge on the same beautiful point: the bitterness is a mercy. Ibn Kathir says Allah made the sea's water salty *lest the air turn putrid because of them and the whole earth turn rotten as a result*, and lest the earth spoil because of the animals dying on it. "Because its water is salty, its air is healthy and its dead are good (to eat)." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops the same reasoning: the oceans cover about two-thirds of the globe while the remaining third is the land mass on which people live; the creatures living in sea water are many times more numerous than those on land, and they die in it. Were that vast body of water sweet, their decomposition would contaminate it, marine life could not survive, and the stench would be unbearable for life on land. The land's rubbish, too, is generally dumped in the sea and decomposed there. So the water you cannot drink is precisely the water that lets you breathe.

Ibn Kathir then attaches a ruling to this natural fact. Because the sea's water is salt, its air is healthy and its dead are wholesome — and so, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked whether sea water can be used for wuḍūʼ, he said: **"Its water is pure and its dead are lawful."** Ibn Kathir notes that this was recorded by Mālik, ash-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad, and by the scholars of Sunan, with a good (*jayyid*) chain of narration. Notice what has happened: a sign in nature, an explanation of its wisdom, and a point of fiqh — sea water purifies, and what dies in it is lawful to eat — all held together in one ayah's worth of reflection.

**The barrier.** *Barzakh* (بَرْزَخ), says Ibn Kathir, means a partition — and here that partition is dry land. And *ḥijran maḥjūran* (حِجْرًا مَّحْجُورًا) he glosses as a barrier that prevents one of them from reaching the other. He reads the ayah beside its sisters: "He has let loose the two seas meeting together. Between them is a barrier which none of them can transgress. Then which of the blessings of your Lord will you both deny?" (55:19–21), and "...and set a barrier between the two seas. Is there any god with Allah?" (27:61).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a second layer. Beyond the visible partition of land, it points to a further "perfect demonstration of His complete power": when a river of sweet water falls into the sea, the two waters do not mingle immediately where they meet, but stay separated for miles — *despite the fact that there is no physical curtain between them*. A barrier you cannot see is still a barrier, and it holds because He holds it.

## Ayah 54: from a drop of water to a whole society

**"And it is He Who has created man from water, and has appointed for him kindred by blood, and kindred by marriage. And your Lord is Ever All-Powerful to do what He wills."**

Ayah 53 was water in the earth; ayah 54 is water in you. Ibn Kathir explains "created man from water" as: He created him from a weak *nuṭfah*, "then gave him shape and formed him, and completed his form, male and female, as He willed."

Then the astonishing turn. From that one beginning Allah draws out an entire web of belonging. Ibn Kathir traces the arc of an ordinary life: "in the beginning, he is someone's child, then he gets married and becomes a son-in-law, then he himself has sons-in-law and other relatives through marriage. All of this comes from a despised liquid."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines the two terms precisely:

- **nasab** (نَسَب) — kinship of blood: the relationship which emanates from either parent.
- **ṣihr** (صِهْر) — kinship of in-laws: the kinship which is drawn from the wife's side.

And it draws out why this counts as a favour at all: "All these relations and bonds are Allah's graces given to mankind for a pleasant and tranquil life. If these relations are taken away from someone's life it will be impossible for him to live by himself." Strip a person of parents, siblings, spouse and in-laws, and you have not merely made him lonely; you have made his life unliveable. The ayah then names the quality behind it all: **"And your Lord is Ever All-Powerful to do what He wills."** The same power that keeps two waters from merging builds a family out of a drop.

## Ayah 55: and yet they worship what does nothing

**"And they worship besides Allah, that which can neither profit them nor harm them; and the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord."**

Set this against what has just been described and the sheer irrationality lands. Ibn Kathir says Allah is telling us how ignorant the idolaters are: instead of worshipping Allah they worship idols which possess no power to harm or benefit — and they do it "with no evidence or proof; the only thing that led them to do this was their own whims and desires."

Worse, the relationship runs backwards. They take these idols as protectors and fight for their sake, and they oppose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and the believers for their sake. Ibn Kathir quotes: "And they have taken besides Allah gods, hoping that they might be helped. They cannot help them, but they will be brought forward as a troop against those who worshipped them" (36:74–75). The worshippers imagine themselves defended; in reality they are the garrison. As Ibn Kathir puts it, these ignorant people are troops for the idols and are ready to fight for their sake and protect their sanctuaries.

The last phrase, *"and the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord,"* is startling. Ibn Kathir explains it as: he is a supporter of Shayṭān against the party of Allah — and Mujāhid said, "He supports and helps the Shaytan in disobedience towards Allah." A creature enlisting on the opposing side against his own Maker. But Ibn Kathir does not leave the reader anxious: the party of Allah are the ones who will prevail — "in the end the victory will be for Allah and His Messenger and the believers, in this world and the Hereafter."

## Ayah 56: what the Messenger ﷺ actually is

**"And We have sent you only as a bearer of good news and a warner."**

Two words define the office: *mubashshiran* (مُبَشِّرًا), a bearer of good news, and *nadhīran* (نَذِيرًا), a warner. Ibn Kathir: "a bringer of good news to the believers, a warner to the disbelievers; bringing good news of Paradise to those who obey Allah, and bringing warnings of a dreadful punishment for those who go against the commandments of Allah."

The word "only" is doing quiet work. The office is defined by a limit — announcing and warning is the whole of the commission. What is done with the announcement is left, as the very next ayah says, to "whosoever wills."

## Ayah 57: the messenger who charges nothing

**"Say: 'No reward do I ask of you for this, save that whosoever wills may take a path to his Lord.'"**

Ibn Kathir puts the words in the Prophet's mouth: for conveying this message and this warning, "I do not ask for any reward from your wealth; I am only doing this for the sake of Allah, may He be exalted." He reads the exception — *whosoever wills may take a path to his Lord* — as "a way and a methodology to be followed," and sets beside it "To whomsoever among you who wills to walk straight" (81:28).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the tenderness in the construction. The Prophet ﷺ was told to say that he has no personal interest in this invitation and seeks no reward from the people for his efforts. **"His reward is only that they turn towards Allah."** And, it adds, "it is but obvious that if someone moves to the righteous path it is he who will be the gainer" — so the "payment" he names is in fact a further gift to the payer. The commentary offers a homely image: it is just like an old father asking his children to eat and drink and be merry, and declaring to them that their eating and drinking is a reward for himself. Such was his love for the people; he "considered the gain of the people as his own."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) adds a second possibility: the right conduct of the people may itself be a reward for the Prophet ﷺ, because he too is rewarded when they take up the right path. It notes that some authentic traditions say that when someone calls people to the righteous path and they respond, the reward goes not only to those who acted righteously but also to the one who persuaded them.

## Ayah 58: where the caller rests his weight

**"And put your trust in the Ever Living One Who dies not, and glorify His praises, and sufficient is He as the All-Knower of the sins of His servants."**

A man who takes no fee and controls no outcome needs somewhere to stand. Ayah 58 gives it. Ibn Kathir: in *all* your affairs, put your trust in Allah, the Ever-Living Who never dies. He gathers Allah's other descriptions around it — the One who "is the First and the Last, the Most High and the Most Near. And He is the All-Knower of everything" (57:3); "the Eternal, Ever-Lasting, Ever-Living, Self-Sufficient One, the Lord and Sovereign of all things, the One to Whom you should always turn." Allah is the One in whom you should put your trust and to whom you should turn for refuge; "He will be sufficient for you and will be your helper and supporter, and will cause you to prevail" — as He said to His Messenger ﷺ, "Allah will protect you from mankind" (5:67).

A contrast runs under the surface of the passage: in ayah 55 they lean on what "can neither profit them nor harm them"; in ayah 58 he is told to lean on the Ever-Living Who dies not.

**"And glorify His praises."** Ibn Kathir reads *wa sabbiḥ bi-ḥamdih* as an instruction to *combine* the two: "combine praising Him with glorifying Him." Hence, he notes, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: *"Subḥānaka Allāhumma Rabbanā wa bi-ḥamdik"* — "Glory be to You, O Allah, and with Your praise." The meaning of the ayah, Ibn Kathir says, comes to this: **be sincere in worshipping Him and putting your trust in Him** — the pairing found also in "So worship Him and put your trust in Him" (11:123), "there is no god but He, so take Him as a Trustee" (73:9), and "Say: He is the Most Gracious, in Him we believe, and in Him we put our trust" (67:29).

**"And sufficient is He as the All-Knower of the sins of His servants."** Ibn Kathir: "by His perfect knowledge nothing is hidden from Him nor can anything be hidden from Him, not even a speck of dust's weight." Read in the flow of the passage this is at once relief and warning: the Prophet ﷺ need not prosecute his opponents' inner wrongs, because Allah's knowledge of them is sufficient; and no servant, ourselves included, should imagine anything is being missed.

## Living it

- **Look at ordinary water.** The passage builds its case not on marvels but on the well, the river, the sea. Ibn Kathir says Allah told us these realities "so that His servants may realize His blessings to them and give thanks to Him." Reflection here is not decoration; it is the intended response.
- **Treat family as a favour, not furniture.** Ayah 54 counts blood kin and in-laws among Allah's graces for "a pleasant and tranquil life" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is blunt that without such bonds it would be impossible to live by oneself. Both kinds of kinship are named in one breath; both are given, and both are owed something.
