- **Ask what you are actually serving.** Ayah 55 exposes false worship as expensive: loyalty and conflict spent defending what "can neither profit them nor harm them." The test is whether the thing you are defending can do anything for you at all.
- **Invite without a price tag.** Ayah 57 sets the standard for anyone who calls others to good: no fee, no personal interest, satisfaction taken in the other person's gain — with the encouragement that the one who persuades another towards the righteous path shares in the reward.
- **Anchor the day in trust and glorification.** Ayah 58 pairs them: rely on the Ever-Living Who dies not, and keep the tongue moving with *Subḥānaka Allāhumma Rabbanā wa bi-ḥamdik*. Ibn Kathir's summary joins the two — be sincere in worshipping Him, and in putting your trust in Him.

passages.title: Who is the Most Compassionate? Creation answers
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat put a question and an answer side by side. Allah introduces Himself as the Creator of the heavens and the earth who then rose over the Throne — **Ar-Rahman**, the Most Compassionate (ayah 59). The idolaters hear that Name and push it away: "And what is Ar-Rahman?" (ayah 60). Allah does not argue; He points upward. The stars, the sun, the moon, the endless turning of night into day (ayat 61–62) answer the question the deniers refused to have answered. What holds the passage together is that one Name: it is announced, it is rejected, and then the whole sky is called as witness to it.

## The argument these ayat are answering

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 59 as the continuation of what comes just before. Allah has been describing how ignorant the idolaters are: they leave Allah and worship idols that "do not possess the power either to harm or benefit," with no evidence or proof, driven only by their own whims and desires. They take those idols as protectors, fight for their sake, and oppose Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers — hence "the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord." Mujahid explained that phrase to mean: he supports and helps Shaytan in disobedience towards Allah. Ibn Kathir adds the sobering irony that such people become troops for their idols, ready to fight for their sake and protect their sanctuaries, while in the end the victory will be for Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers, in this world and the Hereafter.

Against that background the Prophet ﷺ is told what he is and is not: "We have sent you only as a bearer of good news and a warner" — good news of Paradise for those who obey Allah, warning of a dreadful punishment for those who go against His commandments. He is told to say he asks no payment for the message: as Ibn Kathir puts it, *for conveying this message and this warning I do not ask for any reward from your wealth; I am only doing this for the sake of Allah.* The only "reward" he wants is that "whosoever wills may take a path to his Lord" — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, a way and a methodology to be followed.

Then comes the command that ayah 59 is built to support: **"Put your trust in the Ever-Living One Who dies not."** Ibn Kathir: in all your affairs, put your trust in Allah, the Ever-Living Who never dies, the Eternal, Ever-Lasting, Self-Sufficient One, the Lord and Sovereign of all things — the One who is "the First and the Last, the Most High and the Most Near" (57:3). He is the One to whom you should always turn; He will be sufficient for you, will be your helper and supporter, and will cause you to prevail. Ibn Kathir sets alongside it: "O Messenger! Proclaim what has been sent down to you from your Lord... Allah will protect you from mankind" (5:67). And "glorify His praises" means, in his words, to combine praising Him with glorifying Him — which is why the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say *Subhanaka Allahumma Rabbana wa bihamdik*, "Glory be to You, O Allah, and with Your praise." The closing phrase of the ayah — "sufficient is He as the All-Knower of the sins of His servants" — means, Ibn Kathir says, that by His perfect knowledge nothing is hidden from Him nor can anything be hidden from Him, not even a speck of dust's weight.

Notice the emotional logic. The one carrying this message, under opposition, is told: the One you are leaning on does not die, does not lose interest, and does not miss a thing. Only then does ayah 59 tell you who exactly that is.

## Ayah 59: the Creator, the Throne, and the Name

"Who created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six Days." Ibn Kathir glosses: He is the Ever-Living Who never dies, the Creator, Sustainer and Sovereign of all things, Who by His might and power created the seven heavens with their vast height and width and the seven earths with their great depths and density.

"**Then He rose over (istawa) the Throne.**" Ibn Kathir's comment on this phrase, in full, is about what it means for the world we live in: *He is running all affairs and He decrees according to the truth, and He is the best of those who decide.* That is the weight of the sentence — the universe is under active, wise, just command.

And immediately: "**Ar-Rahman** — *fas'al bihi khabira*." The One upon the Throne is the Most Compassionate. Power and mercy are not two rival departments; they belong to the same Lord.

That last phrase is rendered in more than one way by the sources, and they can be laid side by side honestly:

- **Ibn Kathir** takes it as "Ask Him, as He is the All-Knower," and explains: find out about Him from the one who knows most about Him, and follow him and take him as your example — and there is no one who knows more about Allah than His servant and Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, the absolute leader of the sons of Adam in this world and the Hereafter, who does not speak of his own desire but conveys revelation revealed to him. From this Ibn Kathir draws a rule of the religion: what he ﷺ says is true, and he is the leader whose decision counts; when there is a dispute, people are obliged to refer to him (as in 4:59, and "in whatsoever you differ, the decision thereof is with Allah," 42:10); whatever is in accordance with his words and deeds is right, and whatever goes against them should be rejected no matter who says or does it. And "the Word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice" (6:115) — meaning, He has spoken the truth and is fair and just in His commands and prohibitions.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān**, citing Mazhari, takes it as "So ask about Him someone who knows": the creation of the earth and the skies, and then His rising over the Throne in consonance with His exalted position, are all acts of Allah; whoever wants confirmation should find out from those who know the truth — and the "one who knows" here may be Allah Himself, or Jibra'il (peace be upon him), or possibly the scholars of the previous Books, in which this truth was also mentioned.

Either way the instruction is the same in spirit: this is not a matter to be settled by your own guesswork. Go to the source that actually knows.

## Ayah 60: "And what is Ar-Rahman?"

Ibn Kathir reads their reply as a refusal dressed up as a question: *we do not know Ar-Rahman* — and, as he says a second time, *we do not know or approve of this Name*. They did not like to call Allah by His Name Ar-Rahman. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens it with a linguistic fact: *Rahman* is an Arabic word and all Arabs knew its meaning; they simply did not use it for Allah. Their difficulty was not vocabulary. It was that they refused to use this word **for Allah**. So their "what is Ar-Rahman?" was not a request for a definition; it was a way of not conceding the Name.

Ibn Kathir connects this to a scene the reader can picture. He notes that they objected in the same way on the day of the treaty of Al-Hudaybiyyah, when the Prophet ﷺ told the scribe to write *Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim*, and they said: "We do not know Ar-Rahman or Ar-Rahim. Write what you used to write: *Bismika Allahumma* — in Your Name, O Allah." (Ibn Kathir relates this incident without naming a collection, so it is passed on here exactly as he passes it on.) It is the same attitude the ayah describes, put down in writing on a treaty document. And Ibn Kathir says it was then that Allah revealed: "Say: Invoke Allah or invoke Ar-Rahman, by whatever name you invoke Him, to Him belong the Best Names" (17:110) — meaning, He is Allah and He is the Most Gracious; these are not two.

"**Shall we fall down in prostration to that which you command us?**" Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is one line and it exposes the whole disease: *"Just because you tell us to."* Their objection is not to the evidence; it is to being told. Pride refuses the posture before it examines the claim. And the result is the last phrase — "**and it increases in them only aversion**."

Ibn Kathir sets the believers directly opposite them: they worship Allah Who is the Most Gracious, Most Merciful, they attribute divinity to Him alone, and they prostrate to Him. And he records that the scholars agree it is allowed and approved for the reader and the listener to prostrate when reaching this mention of prostration in Surat al-Furqan, and Allah knows best. So the ayah that reports a refusal to prostrate invites you to go down and do it — the shortest possible reply to "shall we prostrate just because we are told?"

## Ayat 61–62: creation gives the answer

The reply to "what is Ar-Rahman?" is not a debate. It is: **"Tabaraka — Blessed be He Who has placed in the heaven Al-Buruj."** Ibn Kathir says Allah is here glorifying Himself and praising the beauty He created in the heavens.

- **Al-Buruj.** Ibn Kathir reports these as the giant stars, according to the view of Mujahid, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Abu Salih, al-Hasan and Qatadah — comparable to "And indeed We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps" (67:5).
- **Sirajan — "a great lamp."** This is the sun, which shines like a lamp, as in "And We have made a shining lamp" (78:13).
- **Qamaran munira — "a moon giving light."** Ibn Kathir is precise: shining and *illuminated by the light of something else*, different from the light of the sun. He cites "It is He Who made the sun a shining thing (*diya'*) and the moon a light (*nur*)" (10:5), and Nuh (peace be upon him) saying to his people, "has He not made the moon a light therein, and made the sun a lamp?" (71:15–16). The two are given different words because they are not described as doing the same thing.

Then ayah 62: "**And He it is Who has put the night and the day in succession — *khilfatan*.**" Ibn Kathir: each one comes after the other in a never-ending alternation; when one goes the other comes, and vice versa — "the sun and the moon, both constantly pursuing their courses" (14:33), "He brings the night as a cover over the day, seeking it rapidly" (7:54), "it is not for the sun to overtake the moon" (36:40). Mujahid and Qatadah added a second sense of *khilfatan*: that the two are **different** from one another, because one is dark and the other is light. Both senses live in the one word: they follow each other, and they are unlike each other.

## The mercy folded into the clock

Why answer a question about *Ar-Rahman* with a description of sunrise and sunset? Because the alternation is itself an act of compassion. Ibn Kathir explains "for whoever desires to remember or desires to show his gratitude" this way: Allah has caused them both to follow one another to show the times when His servants should worship Him — **so whoever misses an act of worship during the night can make it up during the day, and whoever misses an act of worship during the day can make it up during the night.**

The turning of the sky is, in other words, a standing second chance. Ibn Kathir supports this with a hadith he records as authentic (*Sahih*), citing it without naming a collection: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, spreads forth His Hand at night for the one who has done evil during the day to repent, and spreads forth His Hand during the day for the one who has done evil during the night to repent. That is the answer to "what is Ar-Rahman?" — a Lord who arranges the calendar of the universe around the possibility of your return.

## What the passage asks of you

Ayah 62 does not say night and day were made for everyone equally. It says they were made "**for whoever wishes to remember, or wishes to show gratitude**." The benefit is conditional on a desire. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it bluntly: Allah created the sun, the moon and the stars which bring about day and night in turn, so that those who give thought to the things around them should see the manifestation of His omnipotence and the proof of His Oneness, and so that the thanks-givers should have occasion for thanks-giving — therefore whoever pays no heed to the manifestation of His creation and offers Him no gratitude lives a useless life, and has lost his capital as well. Maʿārif follows this with a prayer worth borrowing: *Allahumma-jʿalna min adh-dhakirin ash-shakirin* — O Allah, make us among those who remember You and those who thank You.

On that "lost capital," Maʿārif quotes Ibn al-ʿArabi, who says he heard from the one he calls the Great Martyr: a man who reaches sixty and has spent half of it — thirty years — in sleep, and a sixth of it, ten years, resting during the daytime, is in great loss; he has spent only twenty years of his life in working. The point is not the arithmetic. It is that the days are being spent whether or not you are noticing them, and remembrance and gratitude are what turn time into capital.

Practically, this passage sets three things in front of you: prostrate where they refused to (the sajdah of Surat al-Furqan); lean on the Ever-Living Who does not die rather than on anything that dies; and use the next turn of night or day to make up what you owe, rather than treating a missed act of worship as a closed file.

## How to read these ayat about the sky

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses at ayah 61 for an extended discussion, because "He placed constellations *in the sky*" is where people rush to make the Qur'an take sides in astronomy. Its guidance is worth having:

**The Qur'an is not a book of philosophy or astronomy.** It mentions the earth, the sky, the stars and their movements repeatedly, but always so that a person may set his beliefs right and understand that this spectacular phenomenon did not come into being on its own — there is Someone who created it, and that Someone is Allah. For that, Maʿārif says, no special philosophical knowledge or research data is required. An ordinary person who watches the days lengthen and shorten, the seasons turn, the moon wax and wane, the eclipses arrive, all with perfect precision and without the slightest alteration for centuries, can draw the conclusion the Qur'an wants: there is a Power who created it and is running and holding it. Maʿārif notes that the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions made no arrangement to study astronomical or cosmic theories, although people in Egypt, Syria, India and China had already worked on these subjects — which shows that mastering cosmology was never the objective of these ayat.

**"In the sky" carries two possible senses.** Maʿārif observes that the Arabic *sama'* is used in the Qur'an in two ways: for the great mass of the sky — spoken of as an enclosure with gates guarded by angels — and for everything above us in that direction, including the atmosphere and space. When Allah says He sent down purifying water "from the heavens" (25:48), the second sense is clearly meant, since the Qur'an itself says in express terms that the rain comes from the clouds (56:69; 78:14). So "constellations in the sky" may mean placed in the mass of the sky, or placed in the space above us. In the presence of these two possibilities, no absolute declaration on the question can be attributed to the Qur'an.

**Hence the rule of interpretation.** Maʿārif states that classical and modern religious scholars are unanimous on this: where a statement in the Qur'an is lucid and unambiguous, it is not permissible to twist its wording to bring it into line with any theory, old or new — the theory is then to be regarded as based on some misconception. But where the Qur'an gives no express statement and more than one interpretation is possible from the wording, the interpretation closer to observation and evidence is regarded as correct. Reading ayah 61 as stars in space, on that basis, is not tantamount to twisting the Qur'anic statement; it is only the adoption of one of the two possible interpretations. What could not be accepted, Maʿārif adds, is the claim that the skies do not exist, since the Qur'an has clearly stated in several verses that the sky is an enclosure with gates guarded by angels.

Maʿārif cites Sayyid Mahmud Shukri Alusi — grandson of Sayyid Mahmud Alusi Baghdadi, author of *Ruh ul-Maʿani* — who examined many principles of modern astronomy and found them not in conflict with the Qur'anic text or the Sunnah, adding that if any of them did differ, we would discard the theory rather than twist the meaning of the texts, "because the sound reason can never be against an authentic text; rather they are complimentary to each other."

Two failures are named, and both refused: the modernist who makes space travel and scientific discovery the very objective of the Qur'an, and the conservative who holds such discoveries to be repugnant to it. Maʿārif's verdict is that these issues are not the subject matter of the Qur'an; what is proved by experiment or observation cannot be taken as contradicting it, and what is not yet proved should not be imposed on it through fanciful interpretations. And it offers one reminder of proportion: enormously costly missions brought back dust and stones from the moon, while the real benefit of such discoveries — to believe in Allah and be grateful to Him — never needed such extraordinary efforts, and can be drawn even by the simplest person through simple observation of these very objects.

Which returns us to the passage. They asked, "And what is Ar-Rahman?" — and the answer was hanging over their heads every night of their lives.

passages.title: Servants of the Most Compassionate: humility, night prayer, balance
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat begin the closing portrait of Sūrah al-Furqān: a description of the people Allah calls, with unmatched honour, **"the servants of the Most Compassionate."** What holds them together is not a list of unrelated virtues but one life seen from several angles — how such a person walks among people, how he answers insult, how he spends his nights, what he fears, and how he handles his money.

## Why this portrait comes here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the placement. Up to this point the sūrah has mostly been occupied with the proofs of the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ and with answering the objections raised by the disbelievers and pagans — and, along the way, with Allah's wrath and punishment on those who reject His commands. Now, at the very end, the sūrah turns to the other side: to those special servants of His who firmly believe in the Prophet's ﷺ prophethood, whose beliefs, deeds and dealings all conform to the will of Allah and His Messenger, and who follow the Sharīʿah. After all the argument, Allah shows us what a person who accepts the message actually looks like.

Maʿārif counts **thirteen traits** of these favoured servants across the closing verses of the sūrah. Our passage, ayat 63–67, gives the first six.

## "Servants of the Most Compassionate"

Being called Allah's own slaves is itself the honour. The word **ʿibād** (عِبَاد) is the plural of **ʿabd**, and Maʿārif is precise about the sense: not "servant" in the mild modern sense, but the slave who is the property of his Master — his deeds, his prerogatives, his very life dedicated to the Master's command and will. Only that person can claim the title whose views and beliefs, whose thinking and desires, whose deeds and actions are all in line with what his Rabb commands and is pleased with, and who keeps himself alert to carry out each command the moment it reaches him.

There is a distinction worth holding on to here. In one sense every creature is Allah's servant, governed by His will with no say in the matter. What ayah 63 is honouring is something else: **voluntary servanthood** — surrendering completely to Allah and bringing every deed and desire into line with His pleasure *by one's own choice*.

And notice which of His names Allah chooses for this title. Out of all His beautiful names and attributes, He says "servants of **al-Raḥmān** — the All-Merciful." Maʿārif suggests the hint is deliberate: being the slaves of the All-Merciful, these people should reflect and demonstrate the quality of mercifulness in the way they deal with everyone. That single observation explains almost everything that follows — the gentle walk, the soft answer, the restrained hand.

## Walking on the earth *hawnan* (ayah 63)

**"Those who walk on the earth *hawnan*."** Ibn Kathir explains: they walk with dignity and humility, not with arrogance and pride — as Allah says elsewhere, *"And walk not on the earth with conceit and arrogance"* (17:37). Maʿārif gives the same range for **هَوْن (hawn)**: humbleness, modesty, decorum; a walk with no pride in it.

Both commentaries then rush to close off a misunderstanding, and it is one of the most useful passages in the whole section. This does **not** mean walking slowly, feebly, like a sick man, as a display of piety. Ibn Kathir writes plainly: it does not mean they should walk like sick people, making a show of their humility — for the leader of the sons of Adam, the Prophet ﷺ, used to walk as if he were coming downhill, and as if the earth were folded up beneath him. Maʿārif confirms from the books of his biography that the Prophet's ﷺ walk was on the quicker side, and cites the wording recorded in a hadith: *"He used to walk in a manner as if the ground was shrinking for him"* (Maʿārif gives this citing Ibn Kathir; no collection is named in these sources, so we should not attach one).

For this reason, Maʿārif reports, the righteous elders described the slow, invalid's walk as a **symbol of arrogance**, an affected habit, and something disliked (makrūh). And there is a memorable illustration, which Maʿārif also relates citing Ibn Kathir: Sayyidnā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) once saw a young man walking very slowly and asked him, "Are you sick?" The young man said no. So ʿUmar raised his stick at him and ordered him to walk robustly.

So what *is* hawn? Ibn Kathir's answer is a pair of words: **serenity and dignity** — the calm, unhurried composure the Arabic calls *sakīna*. He supports it with the Prophet's ﷺ instruction that when you come to the prayer you should not come rushing in haste; come calmly and with tranquillity, and whatever you catch of the prayer, pray it, and whatever you missed, complete it afterwards. (Ibn Kathir gives the Prophet's ﷺ words here without naming a collection.) A man may hurry — the Prophet ﷺ walked briskly — and still carry himself with composure. Hawn is a quality of the heart showing in the body, not a performance staged for onlookers.

Maʿārif adds a beautiful reading from **Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**, which it likewise relates citing Ibn Kathir: the limbs of sincere believers are so humbled before Allah that a stranger might think they are ill or disabled when in fact they are perfectly fit. What has overtaken them is the awe of Allah, which has not struck others; it is the fear of the Hereafter that keeps them from pointless worldly busyness. Those who have no faith and are absorbed in the world end only in disappointment — they do not get what they wanted here, and they forfeit their share there. And those who treat sustenance as the only reward worth having from Allah while neglecting to live morally have very little understanding, and a great punishment awaits them.

Read together, the two comments are not in tension: the outer bearing is unhurried and dignified, not staged; the inner state is genuine awe.

## The answer to the ignorant (ayah 63)

**"And when the ignorant address them, they say: *salāman*."** Two clarifications from Maʿārif open this up.

First, **"the ignorant" (al-jāhilūn)** does not mean the uneducated. It means the one who *behaves* like an ignorant man — and he may well be a learned person. The verse is about conduct, not qualifications.

Second, **salām** here is not the customary greeting. It stands for any word that produces peace. The meaning, as Mujāhid and Muqātil explain it, is that when met with ignorant speech these servants stay composed and answer calmly, so that the other person is not wounded and they themselves do not fall into sin. In short: they do not take revenge on those who speak to them like fools.

Ibn Kathir puts it in the same terms: if ignorant people insult them with bad words, they do not answer in kind — they forgive, overlook, and say nothing but good. And he adds the highest example: this is exactly what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did — **the more ignorant the people were with him, the more patient he became.** Ibn Kathir links the trait to *"And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it"* (28:55).

## Their nights (ayah 64)

**"Those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing."** Ibn Kathir's comment is that this means worshipping and obeying Him, and he says of such people that **their nights are the best of nights**. He gathers the Qur'an's other descriptions of the same people: *"They used to sleep but little by night, and in the hours before dawn they were asking for forgiveness"* (51:17–18); *"Their sides forsake their beds"* (32:16); *"Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord…"* (39:9).

Why single out the **night**? Maʿārif gives two reasons, and they are worth pausing over:

1. Night is the time set aside for rest, so worship then costs **extra effort** — it is taken from something you genuinely want.
2. It **rules out showing off.** Nobody is watching. Whatever is done in those hours can only be for Allah.

The picture Maʿārif draws is of a complete day: submission to Allah through the daylight hours by teaching and spreading the religion and striving in His path, and through the night by standing before Him in prayer.

**From the Sunnah.** Maʿārif cites Tirmidhī, on the authority of Sayyidnā Abū Umāmah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Remain steadfast to your night prayers, as this has been the practice of all righteous people before your time, and this will bring you closer to Allah Taʿālā, will expiate evils and will keep you away from sins."* (Maʿārif reports this through Mazharī.)

**And a mercy for those who cannot manage much.** Maʿārif then reports two things that widen the door considerably:

- Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said that whoever offers two or more rakʿats after the ʿIshāʾ prayer is also **included in this verse** (Maʿārif, from Mazharī citing Bayhaqī).
- Sayyidnā ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that one who prays ʿIshāʾ in congregation is counted as having worshipped **half the night**, and one who prays Fajr in congregation as having spent **the other half** in prayer (Maʿārif, from Mazharī, citing Aḥmad and Muslim).

This is not a lowering of the ideal — ayah 64 still describes people whose nights belong to Allah. It is an invitation: two rakʿats after ʿIshāʾ already puts your name in this verse, and the two congregational prayers at the two ends of the night can carry the whole night between them.

## The prayer of fear (ayat 65–66)

**"Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; its punishment is unrelenting. It is truly an evil place to settle and to stay."**

Notice where this sits. These are people who stand in prayer at night — and their recorded speech to Allah is not a claim but a plea for rescue. Maʿārif draws exactly that lesson: despite their constant worship day and night, these favoured servants **do not sit content and secure**; they remain fearful of Allah, keeping the Day of Judgment before their eyes, and so they keep both things alive at once — righteous deeds *and* supplication. The safety of these servants is that they never assume they are safe.

The word rendered "unrelenting" is **غَرَامًا (gharām)**. Ibn Kathir explains it as ever-present and never-ending. **Al-Ḥasan** said about it: anything that strikes a son of Adam and then passes is not *gharām*; the inseparable, permanent punishment is the one that lasts as long as the heavens and the earth. Ibn Kathir notes that **Sulaymān al-Taymī** held the same view. That is why the plea is so urgent: this is not a hardship you survive and then leave behind.

Ayah 66 is still part of their prayer: *"how evil it is as a place to dwell, and how evil as a place to rest"* — Ibn Kathir reads **مُسْتَقَرًّا (mustaqarr)** as an abode to settle in and **مُقَامًا (muqām)** as a place to stay. The two words together name what a home is supposed to give — settlement and rest — and deny both to the Fire.

## Neither wasteful nor tight-fisted (ayah 67)

The sixth trait moves from the night prayer to the wallet, and the Qur'an treats the two as belonging to the same character.

**Isrāf (إسراف)** means to cross the limit. Maʿārif reports two explanations. According to Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujāhid, Qatādah and Ibn Jurayj, **any spending on something sinful, however small, is isrāf.** Others say that even overspending on lawful, rightful things — spending that is simply wasteful — falls under isrāf, since wasteful spending is itself a sin; Allah says, *"Surely the squanderers are brothers of the devils"* (17:27). Maʿārif notes that on that reasoning the second explanation is really contained within the first: waste is a sin, and spending on sin is isrāf.

**Iqtār (إقتار)** is the opposite failing: to spend with miserliness. In the language of Islamic jurisprudence, Maʿārif explains, it means being tight-fisted precisely where a believer has been directed to spend — and to spend **nothing at all** where one has been commanded to spend is the worst case of it. This too is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) and Qatādah.

Ibn Kathir puts the same balance in domestic terms: they are not extravagant, spending beyond what they need, nor are they miserly **towards their own families**, failing to spend enough on their needs — they take the best and fairest way, because the best of matters are the moderate ones, neither extreme. He connects it to the image in *"And do not keep your hand chained to your neck, nor stretch it out to its fullest reach"* (17:29): a fist clamped shut and an arm flung wide are both deformities of the same hand.

The passage's own word for the goal is **قَوَامًا (qawāman)** — "a just balance between them." It is not a grudging compromise between two goods; it is the upright standard, with waste on one side of it and stinginess on the other.

**From the Sunnah on moderation.** Maʿārif quotes a saying of the Prophet ﷺ: *"It is part of a man's sound understanding that he takes the middle path in his spending."* And in another, reported by Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him), the Prophet ﷺ said: *"He who is moderate in spending will never become destitute"* — this second one Maʿārif attributes to Imām Aḥmad, via Ibn Kathir. (For the first, no collection is named in our sources, so none should be claimed for it.)

## Living it

Set the six traits side by side and a single character emerges:

- **A bearing that is calm without being staged** — no swagger, and no performed feebleness either. Move briskly if you need to; carry serenity and dignity while you do.
- **A mouth that refuses to escalate.** When someone behaves ignorantly — learned or not — the reply is whatever word restores peace: not because you lost the argument, but because you will not sin and will not wound.
- **A night that belongs to Allah**, even if it begins with two rakʿats after ʿIshāʾ, and is anchored by ʿIshāʾ and Fajr in congregation.
- **Fear that survives your own good deeds.** The night-worshippers of ayah 64 are the ones begging in ayah 65. Worship is never a receipt.
- **A hand that is neither chained nor flung open** — generous where Allah has directed you to give, especially to your own household, and never spending on sin, however little.

And over all of it, the title in ayah 63: these are the slaves of **al-Raḥmān**. The mercy they have received is meant to be visible in how they walk, how they answer, and how they give.

passages.title: The three grave sins and the door of repentance
passages.tafsir:
This passage names the three gravest sins a human being can commit — setting up a rival to Allah, killing a soul Allah has made sacred, and unlawful sexual intercourse — states the terrible end of the one who does them, and then, in a single word of exception, throws open a door that no sin can hold shut. Ayat 68 and 69 are the warning; ayat 70 and 71 are the mercy. They belong together: the severity of the first half is what makes the generosity of the second half so startling.

## Where these ayat sit in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the structure. The passage on the servants of the Most Gracious has already listed six qualities, and those first six were all matters of **obedience** — the principles of what these servants do. Now the list turns to **disobedience** — what they refuse to do. The seventh characteristic is a matter of belief: they do not associate anyone with Allah in His worship. The eighth and ninth are matters of action: they do not kill a person whom Allah has given sanctity, and they do not commit zina (unlawful sexual intercourse).

Notice the order, and notice what it establishes. The very first thing said about their avoidance of sin concerns creed. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out, this point itself establishes that **shirk — associating anyone with Allah in worship — is the biggest sin of all.**

## The three sins, in the Prophet's ﷺ own ranking

The most striking thing about this list is that the Prophet ﷺ had already given exactly these three, in exactly this order, before the ayah came down.

Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad reported from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked which sin is the most serious. He said: *"That you appoint a rival to Allah when He has created you."* He was asked, "Then what?" He said: *"That you kill your child for fear that he may eat with you."* "Then what?" He said: *"That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife."* ʿAbdullah said, "Then Allah revealed, confirming that: *And those who invoke not any other god along with Allah…*" Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by An-Nasaʼi, and by Al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Read the wording of the three answers closely. None of them is left as a bare category. It is not simply associating a partner with Allah, but doing so **when He has created you**. It is not merely killing, but killing **your child**, and the motive named is *fear that he may eat with you*. It is not merely zina, but with **your neighbour's wife**. In each answer the Prophet ﷺ adds the detail that makes the act what it is.

Then Allah revealed the ayah confirming what His Messenger ﷺ had said.

## Who was actually asking

Ibn Kathir preserves the occasion behind the second half of the passage, and it changes the whole tone of the reading. Saʿid bin Jubayr heard Ibn ʿAbbas say that **some of the people of shirk had killed a great deal and committed zina a great deal.** They came to Muhammad ﷺ and said: *"What you are saying and calling people to is good — if only you would tell us that there is a way to expiate for what we have done."*

So these were not bystanders being warned off at a safe distance. By the report's own description they were people already deep in exactly these sins, and what they asked for was a way to expiate what they had done.

The answer came down as this ayah — and, the report adds, along with it the ayah: *Say: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves!"* (39:53).

Hold that in mind. Ayat 68 and 69 are frightening. But they were revealed in answer to men who had asked whether there was a way to expiate what they had done.

## Ayah 68: "except for just cause"

The wording of the second sin is careful: *nor kill such person as Allah has forbidden, **except for just cause***. The sanctity of human life is the rule, and the qualification acknowledges that life may be taken justly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes these servants of Allah as those who do not go even near these sins: they neither indulge in adultery nor kill innocent people.

**"Shall receive Athāma."** The ayah ends the warning with a word the early scholars discussed. Two readings are preserved:

- **A valley in Hell.** ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr said, "Athāma is a valley in Hell." ʿIkrimah also said it refers to valleys in Hell in which those who commit unlawful sexual acts will be punished; this was also narrated from Saʿid bin Jubayr and Mujahid.
- **Punishment itself.** As-Suddi said Athāma referred to punishment, which Ibn Kathir judges **closer to the apparent meaning of the ayah** — an interpretation that, as he puts it, makes it interchangeable with what comes next: *the torment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same two views, attributing the meaning "punishment of sin" to Abu ʿUbaidah, and noting (citing Mazhari) that some other commentators said Athāma is the name of a valley in Hell full of severe and rigorous punishments, quoting sayings in support. This is a genuine difference among the scholars, not a settled point; both readings preserve the same warning.

## Ayah 69: doubled, lasting, and humiliating

Two things are said about the punishment, and Ibn Kathir explains each in a phrase.

*The torment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection* — Ibn Kathir: **"repetitive and intensified."** It is not a single blow but a returning one.

*And he will abide therein in disgrace* — Ibn Kathir: **"scorned and humiliated."** Alongside the torment there is contempt. Some suffering is at least borne with dignity; this is not.

**An important qualification.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues at length that this particular description belongs to those who were disbelievers and also committed these crimes, and not to sinning Muslims. Its reasoning: the Qurʼan and the Sunnah teach that a believer receives only one punishment for one sin, and no increase in intensity applies in the case of believers; the doubling fits the disbeliever, whose first punishment is for disbelief itself and is then doubled where he has also committed such sins. And the ayah says the punishment is perpetual — he is placed there forever, disgraced and condemned. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit: **no believer will be condemned forever in Jahannam, no matter how big a sin he has committed.** Muslims will be taken out once they have completed their term. So the picture in ayah 69 — doubled, intensifying, everlasting — describes those who reject the oneness of Allah and also commit adultery and homicide.

That is a mercy to understand properly. It does not make these sins small for a Muslim. It means the Muslim who falls into them is not being told his case is hopeless.

## Ayah 70: the exception that reopens everything

*Except those who repent and believe, and do righteous deeds.*

Ibn Kathir: those who do these evil deeds will be punished in the manner described — **except** those who repent **in this world** to Allah from all of those deeds, for then Allah will accept their repentance. Three things are named together: turning back (*tawbah*), faith (*īmān*), and righteous action.

**The murderer's repentance.** Ibn Kathir treats this ayah as evidence that **the repentance of the murderer is acceptable**, and he addresses the obvious objection — the ayah in Surat An-Nisaʼ, *And whoever kills a believer intentionally* (4:93). He answers that there is no contradiction: although that ayah was revealed in Madinah, its meaning is general, and it could be interpreted to refer to one who does **not** repent, because our ayah states that forgiveness is for those who repent. He supports this with *Verily, Allah forgives not that partners should be set up with Him, but He forgives what is less than that to whom He wills* (4:48), and notes that in the authentic Sunnah it is reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that the repentance of a murderer is acceptable, as was stated in the story of the person who killed one hundred men and then repented, and Allah accepted his repentance.

## "Allah will change their sins into good deeds"

Then comes one of the most astonishing promises in the Qurʼan: not merely that the sins are erased, but that they are **exchanged** — *for those, Allah will change their sins into good deeds, and Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.* How? The commentators offer two explanations.

**First view — the record is replaced.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) reports this from Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas, Hasan al-Basri, Saʿid ibn Jubair and Mujahid: once they have repented of their past sins and accepted Islam, those sins are taken away from the record, because Allah has promised that when a disbeliever accepts Islam all the sins he committed during his disbelief are pardoned. The previous record, full of evil deeds, is forgiven and scrapped, and replaced with a fresh record of the good and righteous deeds performed after submitting to Islam.

**Second view — the act of repenting converts them.** Ibn Kathir has given another explanation, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises it: when such a person remembers the sins he committed in his former life, he repents and seeks Allah's forgiveness — and this act of repentance replaces those sins with virtues. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that traditions have been quoted in support of this explanation.

Both views are held by serious scholars, and neither is diminished by the other.

### From the Sunnah: the last man out of the Fire

Ibn Kathir cites that Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"I know the last person who will be brought forth from Hell, and the last person who will enter Paradise. A man will be brought and it will be said, 'Take away his major sins and ask him about his minor sins.' So it will be said to him: 'On such and such a day, you did such and such, and on such and such a day, you did such and such.' He will say, 'Yes,' and he will not be able to deny anything. Then it will be said to him: 'For every evil deed you now have one good merit.' He will say: 'O Lord, I did things that I do not see here.'"*

Abu Dharr said: **and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ smiled so broadly that his molars could be seen.** Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim recorded it.

Notice what the man himself says at the end. He is the one who points out what is missing from the record — *I did things that I do not see here.* And the detail Abu Dharr chose to preserve is the Prophet's ﷺ smile as he told it.

### The old man with sunken eyes

Ibn Kathir also cites that Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Abu Jabir heard Makhul say: a very old man with sunken eyes came and said, *"O Messenger of Allah, a man betrayed others and did immoral deeds, and there was no evil deed which he did not do. If his sins were to be distributed among the whole of mankind, they would all be doomed. Is there any repentance for him?"* The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked, *"Have you become Muslim?"* He said, "As for me, I bear witness that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner or associate, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger." The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Allah will forgive you for whatever you have done like that, and will replace your evil deeds with good merits."* The man said, "O Messenger of Allah, even my betrayals and immoral actions?" The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Even your betrayals and immoral actions."* The man went away saying *La ilaha illallah* and *Allahu Akbar*.

Ibn Kathir's conclusion: Allah tells us how His mercy extends to all His creatures, and that whoever among them repents to Him, He will accept his repentance for any sin, great or small — as in *And whoever does evil or wrongs himself but afterwards seeks Allah's forgiveness, he will find Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful* (4:110), *Know they not that Allah accepts repentance from His servants* (9:104), and *Say: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves! Despair not of the mercy of Allah"* (39:53) — for those who repent to Him.

## Ayah 71: why the second mention of repentance is not a repetition

*And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, he turns to Allah truly.*

On the face of it this looks like a repetition of the same subject as ayah 70. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Qurtubi who quotes **al-Qaffal**, explains that this repentance is different and separate from the repentance described in the previous ayah — and points to a single missing word as the clue.

Ayah 70 says *repent **and believe** and do righteous deeds*. That word "believe" means that they accepted Islam; that ayah relates to deniers of the oneness of Allah who had indulged in adultery and homicide and then submitted to Islam. **Ayah 71 has no "and believe."** So it speaks of the repentance of Muslim sinners — those who were already Muslims but by negligence fell into these very sins, then repented sincerely, sought Allah's forgiveness, and kept themselves away from sin. Such repentance by Muslims will be regarded as in order and accepted. Ayah 71 is their door.

**Two senses of "repentance" in one ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the fact that the word *tawbah* appears in both the conditional clause and the principal clause of this sentence, carrying a different weight in each. In the conditional clause (*whoever repents*) it means **verbal repentance**. In the principal clause (*he turns to Allah truly*, *matāban*) it means **practical repentance**, in the sense of correcting one's deeds. So the ayah is saying: the one who repents of his sins **and proves his sincerity by not indulging in them again** is on the right path towards Allah. And the reverse follows plainly: **the one who repents of his past sins but continues to indulge in them is like the one who has not repented.**

On *matāban*, Ibn Kathir's comment on the phrase is simple and reassuring: it means **Allah will accept his repentance**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the passage with a hope: if a Muslim falls into a sin by negligence, then realises he has done wrong, repents, and afterwards keeps himself away from it, his repentance will be accepted by Allah — and it may be hoped that he receives the same benefit described in the previous ayah, that his sins are converted into virtues. It then notes that some rules of tawbah have been mentioned here within the description of Allah's favoured servants, and that the next ayat return to the original subject.

## Living it

**Take the three seriously in their order.** The passage puts creed first, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion from that placement: shirk is the biggest sin of all. Guarding whom you call upon — worshipping Allah alone — is the foundation before any question of conduct.

**Do not measure your sin against Allah's mercy.** The men in Ibn ʿAbbas's report asked whether there was any way to expiate what they had done. The old man in Makhul's report asked whether there was any repentance for a man like the one he described. Neither was turned away.

**But do not mistake the door for a licence.** Ayah 70 names repentance, faith, and righteous deeds together; ayah 71, on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, requires that the turning be proved by not going back to the sin. Repentance declared while the sin continues is, in that reading, like no repentance at all.

**And repent now.** Ibn Kathir's phrasing is precise: those who repent **in this world** to Allah from all of those deeds — for then Allah will accept their repentance. The exception in ayah 70 is offered in this life, on this side of the Day described in ayah 69.

passages.title: Truthful witnesses, godly families, and the final word
passages.tafsir:
This passage brings the long portrait of the servants of the Most Merciful to its close, and with it the whole sūrah. Ayat 72–74 give the last of their qualities — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts them as the tenth through thirteenth characteristics — ayat 75–76 announce what such people are given, and ayah 77 turns from them to face those who refused the message. As Maʿārif puts it, in the last verse the disbelievers "have been warned again of the chastisement on which the Surah is concluded."

## Ayah 72: the company you keep

**"And those who do not bear witness to falsehood."** The word is *al-zūr*, and the classical commentators read the phrase two ways, both of them sound.

The first reading takes *yashhadūna* in its sense of *being present at* something: the servants of the Most Merciful simply do not turn up where falsehood is going on. Ibn Kathir says the falsehood here covers "lies, immorality, disbelief, foul speech and false words," and that "from the context it seems that what is meant... is those who do not attend it or are not present when it happens." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an ordering worth holding on to: **the biggest falsehood is kufr and shirk** — disbelief and associating partners with Allah — "and the next in order comes the common lie and acts of sin."

The early scholars each named the gathering of their own time and place, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports them:

- **Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās** — the festivals, carnivals and field days of the idolaters
- **Sayyidnā Mujāhid** and **Muhammad Ibn Ḥanīfah** — music concerts
- **ʿAmr ibn Qays** — vulgar and cheap dance parties; Ibn Kathir reports him as saying it refers to gatherings of sexual immorality
- **Al-Zuhrī** and **Imām Mālik** — liquor drinking parties

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the key point about this list: "there is no contradiction in all these explanations because all such gatherings come under the definition of assembly of falsehood." And Maʿārif adds, citing Mazharī, that the righteous should avoid such gatherings, "as even an intentional look at them is tantamount to participation in them."

The second reading takes *shahādah* in its courtroom sense: **giving false testimony**, which Ibn Kathir defines as "lying deliberately to someone else." Maʿārif notes this is "one of the possible meaning of the word," and that both the Qurʼan and the Sunnah declare false evidence a great sin.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records, from the Two Sahihs, that Abū Bakrah said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked three times, *"Shall I not tell you of the greatest of major sins?"* They said, "Of course, O Messenger of Allah." He said: *"Associating others in worship with Allah, and disobeying one's parents."* He had been lying down; then **he sat up** and added: *"Beware false speech, and bearing witness to falsehood"* — and he kept repeating it until, Abū Bakrah says, they wished he would stop. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise notes that Bukhārī and Muslim record false evidence being named the gravest of the major sins, and reports (citing Mazharī) that Sayyidnā ʿUmar said a proven false witness should be flogged with forty stripes, his face painted black and taken round the market place, and after that put in jail for a long time.

**"And when they pass by the absurd things, they pass by with dignity."** These servants do not attend such gatherings intentionally, but a road sometimes runs past one. Ibn Kathir: "if it so happens that they pass by it, they do not let it contaminate them in the slightest."

Everything turns on the word **karīman** — rendered "with dignity" by Ibn Kathir, and by Maʿārif as walking away "with dignity and grace." Maʿārif then draws out the edge that is easy to miss: passing this way means that "despite their belief that their evil acts are hateful, they do not take pride or regard themselves superior for not indulging in them."

Maʿārif relates, citing Ibn Kathir, that Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd once happened to pass by an absurd and dissolute gathering, and did not stop there but simply walked away. When the Prophet ﷺ learnt of it he remarked that **"Ibn Masud has become *karīm* (dignified)"** — and then recited this ayah, in which walking away from such gatherings with dignity is enjoined.

## Ayah 73: how they receive the Qurʼan

**"And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind."**

Ibn Kathir reads it by contrast. This, he says, is a characteristic of the believers, the ones described in Sūrah al-Anfāl: "Those who, when Allah is mentioned, feel a fear in their hearts, and when His verses are recited unto them, they increase their faith; and they put their trust in their Lord" (8:2). The disbelievers hear the very same words unmoved — "they are not affected by them or moved to change their ways," but "persist in their disbelief, wrongdoing, ignorance and misguidance," continuing as they were, "as if they did not hear them but are deaf and blind." Ibn Kathir sets alongside it the verse where revelation increases the faith of believers but adds "doubt to their doubt" in those with sickness in their hearts (9:124–125).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the phrase from a second angle. To *fall at* the divine revelation — "to listen them with full attention" — "is a virtuous and commendable act." What is condemned is falling at the verses **deaf and blind**: listening "without any purpose or commitment," acting "in a manner that the real message has not been registered." The blessed servants of Allah, by contrast, "pay heed to them like sober and sensible persons, and act upon them."

**Acting on the Qurʼan without understanding it.** The censure, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, covers not only ignoring the message but also listening and acting on it "without due diligence, that is without comprehending the intent and spirit of the precept and according to one's own sweet will" — where a person's practice "is not in line with the practices of the companions of the Prophet or their followers."

The illustration is a report Ibn Kathir relates on the authority of Ibn ʿAwn, who asked Ḥaḍrat al-Shaʿbī: if he comes across people in the state of *sajdah* (prostration), is it correct for him to join them? Al-Shaʿbī said no — not unless he finds out the purpose of that act. As Maʿārif puts it, "it is not proper for a believer to join in any action without knowing the purport of that act."

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a conclusion about study. It calls it "a matter of great satisfaction" that there is a new tendency among younger and modern-educated people to study the Qurʼan — but warns that trying to grasp it through translations on their own, "being against the correct principles of learning something, often makes them fall into misconceptions." Knowledge, it says, cannot be imparted through books alone "unless guidance of a teacher is available for explaining the intricacies of the subject which normally go unnoticed by an ordinary reader." Maʿārif closes the point with a prayer: "May Allah lead us to the right path."

## Ayah 74: the duʿāʼ of a household

**"Our Lord! Bestow on us from our wives and our offspring the comfort of our eyes, and make us leaders of those who have Taqwa."**

Ibn Kathir explains the request as asking Allah "to bring forth from their loins offspring who will obey Him and worship Him and not associate anything in worship with Him." **Ibn ʿAbbās**: this means offspring "who will strive to obey Allah and bring them joy in this world and the Hereafter." **Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: a man can draw solace from his wife and children if they submit to the way of Allah — "that is the true bliss for a man," and if their good health and wellbeing are added to it, "it is also in order."

The point Maʿārif ul Qurʼān highlights is the reach of the concern: these servants "do not care about correcting themselves only, but also take care of the virtuous actions of their children and spouse, and keep trying for their improvement, and it is a part of their efforts that they pray Allah to make them take the right path."

**A striking illustration.** Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad, through Jubayr ibn Nufayr — noting "its chain of narrators is Sahih, although they did not report it" — that a man passed by while they sat with al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad and exclaimed how blessed were the two eyes that saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, wishing they had seen what he saw. Al-Miqdād became angry, which surprised the narrator, since the man had said nothing but good. Then al-Miqdād turned to him: what makes a man wish to be present when Allah had caused him to be absent, when he does not know how he would have behaved had he been there? By Allah, there are people who *saw* the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Allah will throw them on their faces in Hell, because they did not accept him or believe in him. "Are you not grateful that Allah brought you forth from your mothers' wombs believing in your Lord and in what your Prophet brought, and that the test went to others and not to you?"

He then described that test: Allah sent His Prophet ﷺ "during the most difficult time that any Prophet was ever sent, after a long period of ignorance, when the people could see no better religion than the worship of idols," and he brought **the Criterion which distinguishes truth from falsehood** and which would separate a father from his son. A man would realise that his father, son or brother was a disbeliever, and — Allah having opened his own heart to faith — he knew that if his relative died he would go to Hell, "so he could not rest knowing that his loved one was in the Fire." *That*, al-Miqdād said, is what Allah referred to in this ayah. It reframes the duʿāʼ: "the comfort of our eyes" is asked for by people who know exactly what it costs to love someone who is not upon the truth.

**"And make us leaders of those who have Taqwa."** **Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, al-Suddī, Qatādah and Rabīʿ ibn Anas** explained *imāman* as "leaders who would be taken as examples in good"; others said "guides who would call others to goodness." Ibn Kathir's summary of the motive is beautiful: "they wanted their worship to be connected to the worship of their children and offspring, and their guidance to go beyond themselves and benefit others." This, he says, would be more rewarding and a better end — as recorded in Sahih Muslim from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"When a son of Adam dies, his deeds cease apart from three: a righteous child who will pray for him, knowledge from which others may benefit after him, or ongoing charity."*

**Isn't asking to be a leader a request for status?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the objection honestly: apparently this is a prayer for high status and a source of pride, which other injunctions of the Qurʼan forbid — the final Abode is assigned "to those who intend neither haughtiness on earth nor mischief" (28:83). The answers given:

- **Some scholars**: everyone is already the head or imam of his family; so if his family members become mindful of Allah, he will automatically be their imam. "The prayer was not meant for personal aggrandizement, but for the family members to follow the right path."
- **Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī**: the prayer is not for a high position or authority for oneself, but to request "such a disposition that people try to emulate it in religious deeds and actions" — of benefit to others, and so bringing the one who prayed some share of its reward.
- **Makḥūl al-Shāmī**: the purpose is to implore an exalted status of mindfulness of Allah, such that even those already mindful of Him may draw inspiration to follow it.

**Qurṭubī**, having related the last two, comments that the net outcome of both is the same: to desire an elevated position "in religious affairs for attaining reward in the Hereafter is not improper; rather it is allowed." What 28:83 condemns is "the desire and search for worldly exaltation and authority." This duʿāʼ teaches a believer to want to be worth imitating rather than to want to be admired.

With this, Maʿārif notes, the description of the servants of the Most Merciful is complete.

## Ayat 75–76: the high place

**"Those will be rewarded with the highest place because of their patience. Therein they shall be met with greetings and the word of peace and respect — abiding therein; excellent it is as an abode, and as a place to rest in."**

*Al-ghurfah*, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, literally means an **upper storey**. Ibn Kathir explains that the highest place here is Paradise, and reports from **Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddī** that "it was so called because of its elevation." Maʿārif adds, citing al-Bukhārī, Muslim and Mazharī, that the righteous who have special closeness to Allah will be given high chambers in Paradise "which will look like **stars** to common people."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, from Mazharī, that it is narrated in the Musnad of Ahmad, Bayhaqī, Tirmidhī and Ḥākim, on the authority of Sayyidnā Abū Mālik al-Ashʿarī, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "In Paradise there will be such upper Houses that their interior could be seen from outside and the exterior from inside." The Companions asked who would live in them. He replied: **"Those who keep their speech clean and soft, greet every Muslim, feed the poor, and offer Tahajjud prayers at night when others are sleeping."**

**"Because of their patience."** Ibn Kathir's gloss: *ṣabr* here means "their patience in doing what they did."

**"Greetings and the word of peace."** Ibn Kathir: they will be greeted first with words of welcome and honour; peace will be theirs and they will be wished peace, and the angels shall enter unto them from every gate saying, "Peace be upon you for that you persevered in patience! Excellent indeed is the final home!" Maʿārif: beside every other bounty of Paradise, they will have the honour that the angels greet and congratulate them.

**"Abiding therein."** Ibn Kathir: they will settle there and never leave or move or die; they will never exit or even *wish* to move somewhere else — as in "And those who are blessed, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein for all the time that the heavens and the earth endure" (11:108). Then the closing praise, *mustaqarran wa muqāman*: "its appearance is beautiful and it is a good place in which to rest and to dwell."

## Ayah 77: the last word of the sūrah

**"Say: My Lord pays attention to you only because of your invocation to Him. But now you have indeed denied. So the torment will be yours forever."**

Ibn Kathir: Allah "would not care to pay attention to you if you did not worship Him, for He only created mankind to worship Him Alone and to glorify Him morning and evening." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this one "the simplest and straight forward" — because the very purpose of man's creation is worship: "I have not created Jinn and mankind except to worship Me" (51:56). Duʿāʼ, on this reading, is not an optional extra of religion; it is what gives a human being weight at all.

Then the address turns: *faqad kadhdhabtum* — "But now you have indeed denied," addressed, Ibn Kathir says, to the disbelievers. Maʿārif: since they have belied the truth, "you are of no consequence before Him."

**"So it will be *lizāman*."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "the punishment will be inseparable from you," and explains: this rejection and disbelief "have become an integral part of your being and will keep clinging to you until you are thrown in the Fire of Hell forever." Ibn Kathir: "your denial will remain with you forever, i.e., it will lead to your punishment, doom and destruction in this world and the Hereafter." On what it refers to concretely, the early authorities differed:

- **ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, al-Suddī** and others: the day of Badr — a reckoning that came upon the deniers in this very world.
- **Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**: the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Kathir's verdict: **"there is no conflict between the two interpretations."** The consequence begins in this life and completes in the next.

With this the sūrah ends, and Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on it with the words: "all praise and thanks are due to Allah."

## Living it

1. **Choose your gatherings before you have to choose your behaviour.** Ibn Kathir's summary of ayah 72 is that they simply "do not attend where falsehood occurs" — and when the road runs past it anyway, they pass through without being contaminated.
2. **Guard your tongue in testimony.** The Prophet ﷺ sat up to say it.
3. **Hear the Qurʼan as someone who intends to act** — and, as Maʿārif urges, learn it with the guidance of a qualified teacher rather than assembling a religion from your own reading (ayah 73).
4. **Make your family part of your worship**, by effort and by duʿāʼ; let ayah 74 be a prayer you actually say.
5. **Want to be a good example, not a big name.** Qurṭubī's distinction is the safeguard.
6. **Expect it to cost you** — the reward in ayah 75 is explicitly "because of their patience."

And the sūrah's closing word, to believer and denier alike, is about calling upon Allah. That, Maʿārif says, is the very purpose for which we were made.
